107: Generate AI videos from Claude with Higgsfield MCP
108: Generate AI videos from the Higgsfield API
109: CLI and MCP share one account and one credit balance, so switching between them changes the interface, while the account, credits and Assets stay the same. The API is a separate product with its own API key and a prepaid balance in US dollars; it does not use your higgsfield.ai plan credits.
110: What You Need Before Installing
111: You need three things:
112: A paid Higgsfield subscription.
113: A terminal on macOS, Linux or Windows.
114: One package route: curl (macOS and Linux, nothing else required), Homebrew (needs Homebrew) or npm (needs Node.js).
115: A coding agent is optional. If you plan to call the CLI from Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw or Hermes, the agent can run the installation itself. That is covered in the agents section below.
116: How to Install Higgsfield CLI
117: All three methods install the same tool. Pick the one that matches the rest of your setup, because updates go through the same method you installed with.
118: 1. Install with curl (macOS and Linux). The installer may ask for your system password.
119: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/higgsfield-ai/cli/main/install.sh | sh
120: 2. Or install with Homebrew. Later updates: brew update && brew upgrade higgsfield.
121: brew install higgsfield-ai/tap/higgsfield
122: 3. Or install with npm (any platform, including Windows). The package name is @higgsfield/cli.
123: npm install -g @higgsfield/cli
124: 4. Check the version. It prints the release number, for example higgsfield 1.1.26, with a build date.
125: higgsfield version
126: Troubleshooting: wrong version after install. In our test on macOS, the curl installer reported version 1.1.26, but higgsfield version printed an older 1.0.1 left over from an earlier Homebrew install. Running which -a higgsfield listed both copies, and brew upgrade higgsfield fixed the mismatch. If the version check disagrees with the installer, check for a second copy first.
127: How to Sign In and Check Your Account
128: Sign-in works through the browser, the same way any connected app signs in. There is no key to copy.
129: 1. Start the login. The terminal prints "Opening browser for authentication" and waits. If no browser opens, the terminal also prints the path of a local sign-in file to open manually.
130: higgsfield auth login
131: 2. Approve in the browser. A Higgsfield consent page lists what the CLI will access: your email, basic profile, organization membership and permission to remember the login. Click Allow. The browser shows "Device authorized" and the terminal prints "Successfully authenticated".
132: 3. Confirm the account. It prints one line: email, plan name and available credits.
133: higgsfield account status
134: Two related command groups:
135: higgsfield auth token prints the current access token, and higgsfield auth logout deletes it. Treat the token as a secret: do not paste it into prompts, logs, screenshots or source control. The token is kept in a local credentials file and is short-lived, so a "Session expired" message means running auth login again.
136: higgsfield workspace list shows the billing workspaces on the account with plan and balance, and workspace select switches the one that generations are charged to. In our test, a personal account showed one workspace, named Private.
137: How to Generate an Image and Turn It Into Video
138: Generation runs through higgsfield generate create <model_id> --prompt "...". Parameters go in as --name value. Two flags matter from the start. --wait holds the terminal until the job finishes and prints the result link. --json returns machine-readable output: with --wait, the create command returns the full job record; without it, a list of job ids, and generate wait <job_id> --json returns the record later. The example below makes one image and then animates that same image, which is the usual order when a clip has to match an approved frame.
139: 1. Generate the image. Note the id in the response.
140: higgsfield generate create nano_banana_2 --prompt "1980s flash photo on film: a young man with shaggy dark hair in a black glossy leather jacket with a red flame shape painted on the back, seen from behind, turns his head in profile while talking on a payphone on a subway platform. Silver trains on both sides, the left one blurred as it rushes past, a yellow platform edge, chrome pipes with fluorescent lights overhead. No text, no signs." --aspect_ratio 16:9 --wait --json
141: 2. Animate it. The --start-image flag accepts a job id from a previous generation, an upload id or a local file path; local files are uploaded automatically. Seedance 2.5 needs --mode omni_reference for a start image or reference images, because its default text-only mode does not accept media.
142: higgsfield generate create seedance_2_5 --mode omni_reference --start-image <image_job_id> --prompt "Start from the start frame. 1980s film look, handheld, slow push-in. He listens on the payphone, tense. The left train rushes past, the roar drowns the call, he frowns and shouts \"Hello? I can't hear you!\" The train leaves, sudden quiet, he hears the voice, exhales and smiles: \"Yeah... I'm here.\" Train wind moves his hair, window light flickers on his face. No text." --duration 5 --resolution 1080p --wait --wait-timeout 20m --json
143: Your browser does not support the video.
144: 3. Find the result. The JSON includes id, job_type, status, result_url and the params the model actually used. The video record also lists the start image under medias with its role and source link, and adds thumbnail_url. Both files appear in Assets on higgsfield.ai alongside web generations.
145: In our test, the image finished within about a minute at 2752 by 1536 and cost 2 credits. The 5-second video from that image at 1080p completed inside the 20-minute wait and was priced at 80 credits. An earlier text-only video at the same settings ran longer than the default 10-minute wait, so the call ended with "timed out waiting for job" while the job kept running on the server; higgsfield generate get <job_id> showed it as in_progress, and the video link arrived a few minutes later. --wait-timeout 20m raises the waiting limit to 20 minutes. If a generation takes longer, the command can still time out while the job continues on the server.
146: The params block is useful to read once. It shows the defaults you did not set: for the video, 16:9, standard bitrate and audio generation on.
147: How to Check the Cost Before You Generate
148: higgsfield generate cost returns the credit price of a job without creating it. It takes the same model id, parameters and media flags as generate create, so a cost check is the same command with one word changed.

174: Credit costs verified on October 16, 2026 for one account. Prices depend on model, duration and resolution and may change, so the cost command is the way to see the current figure for your settings. Additional generations or alternatives may increase the total. In our test, a 5-second Seedance 2.5 clip at 1080p was priced at 80 credits for a full render and 15 credits with --draft true at the same duration and resolution, which makes draft a cheaper way to preview before the final pass. Two workflows, voice-change and dubbing, do not support cost estimation.
175: Which Models You Can Call From the Terminal
176: The CLI reads the same catalog as the web app. Two commands cover it:
177: higgsfield model list prints every job type with its display name and category.
178: higgsfield model get <model_id> prints one model's parameters: accepted values, defaults, required fields and limits such as how many references it takes.

212: Analysis
213: In our test on October 16, 2026, model list returned 107 entries. The 35+ figure counts models and tools; the catalog lists each mode and variant as a separate entry, such as upscalers, background removers and the Nano Banana Pro modes, which is why the count is higher. Ids can change between releases, so model list is the source to trust. If you see "Unknown model", check the id for typos and run higgsfield model list to find the current identifier.
214: As an example of model get, Seedance 2.5 shows four modes: text to video, reference-based generation (omni_reference), video edit and video extension. The defaults are 5 seconds at 720p with audio on, it accepts up to 50 reference items, and a draft option is priced lower for previews.
215: How to Use Soul ID From the Terminal
216: Soul ID is how Higgsfield handles character consistency. In the CLI it takes three commands.
217: 1. Train the character. Repeat --image for each photo, up to 20 per character, which is the CLI's limit. The flag accepts local paths or upload ids. --soul-cinematic trains the Soul Cinematic variant.
218: higgsfield soul-id create --name <name> --soul-2 --image ./photo1.jpg --image ./photo2.jpg ...
219: 2. Wait for training. Use the id returned by the first command.
220: higgsfield soul-id wait <soul_id>
221: 3. Generate with the character. The same id works in any compatible image model.
222: higgsfield generate create text2image_soul_v2 --prompt "..." --soul-id <soul_id> --wait
223: Characters trained on the web and in the CLI are stored in the same account, so a Soul ID created in the browser can be called from a script the next day. Soul ID helps keep a character's identity consistent across generations; results still vary from shot to shot. Use photos that you own or have permission to use.
224: How to Use the CLI in Scripts and AI Agents
225: Two features make the CLI usable without a person at the keyboard:
226: --json works on every command and returns raw records.
227: Local file paths passed to --image, --video or --audio are uploaded automatically.
228: The examples below require Bash and jq. Without --wait, generate create returns at once with the new job id, so the first loop starts one video job per line in a prompt file and saves the ids:
229: while IFS= read -r prompt; do
230: higgsfield generate create seedance_2_5 \
231: --prompt "$prompt" --duration 5 --json | jq -r '.[]' >> job_ids.txt
232: done < prompts.txt
233: In our test, a call without --wait printed ["251557f4-..."], a one-element list with the job id, and the generation continued on the server. The second loop waits for each saved id and prints its record, including result_url:
234: while IFS= read -r id; do
235: higgsfield generate wait "$id" --json
236: done < job_ids.txt
237: A separate pipeline from the README lists completed results from the whole generation history, including older jobs, which is useful for a quick look but not for collecting one batch:
238: higgsfield generate list --json | jq -r '.[] | select(.status=="completed") | .result_url'
239: Coding agents use the same tool. Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw and Hermes connect to Higgsfield through CLI + Skills, and the agent can run the setup itself: install the package, run auth login for you to approve in the browser, then add the companion skills with npx skills add higgsfield-ai/skills. Skills are preset workflows for tasks such as ads, UGC videos and faceless content, listed on the Skills page. The ready-to-paste setup message is on the CLI page and in the Help Center.
240: Cursor also supports CLI + Skills alongside its marketplace integration. Claude on the web connects through MCP, and ChatGPT uses the official Higgsfield Plugin. Both routes are in How to Generate AI Videos With AI Agents.
241: Who This Is For
242: The CLI fits people who already work in a terminal: developers wiring generation into a build step, technical creators who batch dozens of clips from a prompt file, and anyone running Claude Code, OpenClaw or Hermes who wants the agent to produce images and video without a browser tab. If your workflow is mostly manual and relies on models included in your Unlimited web access, generating on higgsfield.ai may use fewer credits, because Unlimited does not apply through the CLI. If you generate from scripts, the CLI takes the interface out of the loop. Everything it produces lands in the same Assets library, uses the same Soul characters and draws from the same credit balance as the web app and MCP.

245: Got any questions left?
246: Do I need an API key for Higgsfield CLI?
247: No. The CLI signs in through the browser with a regular Higgsfield account and stores the token locally. API keys belong to the Higgsfield API, a separate product.
248: Does Higgsfield CLI use my plan credits?
249: Yes, at standard rates. Unlimited model access and free generations apply only on higgsfield.ai, so CLI generations are charged to the balance.
250: How do I see the price of a generation before running it?
251: Run higgsfield generate cost with the same model id and parameters you would pass to generate create. It prints the credit price without creating a job.
252: Can I turn an image I generated into a video?
253: Yes. Pass the image job id to --start-image on a video model. For Seedance 2.5, add --mode omni_reference, because its default mode is text only.
254: Why did my video command time out?
255: The --wait flag waits 10 minutes by default, and 1080p video can take longer. The job keeps running on the server. higgsfield generate get <job_id> shows its status, and --wait-timeout 20m raises the limit to 20 minutes.
256: Which coding agents work with the CLI?
257: Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw and Hermes can use Higgsfield through CLI + Skills. Cursor also supports CLI + Skills alongside its marketplace integration. Claude on the web uses MCP, while ChatGPT connects through the official Higgsfield Plugin.

28: What is the Higgsfield API, and how do I get started?
29: Higgsfield
30: 4 min
31: Copy page
32: The Higgsfield API lets you generate video and images from your own code: one API key opens every model in the API catalog, and each request is paid in US dollars from a prepaid balance. No plan or subscription is involved: fund the balance, send requests at the rates listed in the catalog, and new requests simply wait once the balance hits zero.
33: How is the API different from my Higgsfield plan?
34: A subscription on higgsfield.ai and the API are two separate products with separate billing. Your plan, credits, and Unlimited access exist only on the website; the API runs on its own account balance in US dollars.
35: How is the API different from my Higgsfield plan?

51: Which models are available through the API?
52: One API key unlocks every model in the API catalog: 50+ current video and image models, including Seedance, Kling, Wan, MiniMax, PixVerse, LTX, and Grok for video and Ideogram, Recraft, and Qwen for images, alongside Higgsfield's own Soul 2, Soul Cinema, DoP, and Marketing Studio Image. The API has its own curated catalog, and the selection may differ from the model lineup on higgsfield.ai.
53: Every model has its own catalog page listing the current rate, supported resolutions and durations, sample code, a short overview, and a side-by-side table of similar models, so picking the right model doesn't require testing each one in code.
54: How do I get started?
55: Sign up for an API account, either as an individual or as a company.
56: Register a payment method and fund your balance.
57: Generate an API key in the console at open.higgsfield.ai. For security, the full key appears only once, so save it right away. Creating a key unlocks 20 concurrent requests.
58: Connect through the Python or TypeScript SDK, or call the REST API directly from any language with an HTTP client, sending requests to api.higgsfield.ai. Each model page carries sample code, and if you work through a coding agent, ready setup prompts for Claude Code, Cursor, and ChatGPT (Codex).
59: Full reference documentation, quickstart guides, and code examples are available at docs.higgsfield.ai.
60: How is API usage billed?
61: Billing is pay-as-you-go from a US dollar balance, and the minimum top-up is $5. Video models are priced per second of output and image models per image; DoP is the exception, priced per generation. Each model has a fixed rate for every configuration: the rate depends on settings like resolution and audio, is listed publicly, and stays the same regardless of how much you top up. An estimate endpoint returns the cost of a request before you run it. Funds expire one year after they are added to the balance. The balance can't go below zero: once it's empty, new requests wait until you add funds, or you can turn on auto top-up so production traffic never stops.
62: You're only charged for generations that finish successfully. If a request fails, its cost returns to your balance automatically.
63: How does generation work?
64: Generation is asynchronous. You submit a request and receive a request ID, then track progress by polling the status or by receiving a webhook when the result is ready. Once the generation completes, you download the output file.
65: How long are generated files stored?
66: Generated output files stay available for at least 7 days after creation and may be removed from Higgsfield servers after that period. For long-term retention, download completed files to your own storage as part of your integration.
67: Where do I see my API spending?
68: Everything lives in the console at open.higgsfield.ai. Analytics shows spend and request volume over time and exports to CSV for reporting; Billing holds your current balance, payment methods, and invoice history.
69: How is the API different from MCP and CLI?
70: MCP and CLI are agent connections: they attach Claude, Cursor, or another agent to your existing higgsfield.ai account, and everything they generate deducts your plan credits. The API doesn't touch your account or credits at all: it runs on its own key and dollar balance, and it's built for shipping generation inside your own product.

88: Got any questions left?
89: Is Open Higgsfield a different product?
90: No. Open Higgsfield is the name of the API console at open.higgsfield.ai. The product, the catalog, and the billing are the same Higgsfield API.
91: Can I use the API without a Higgsfield plan?
92: Yes. The API works entirely on its own dollar balance. Having or not having a plan on higgsfield.ai changes nothing about API access or rates.
93: Can I use content generated through the API commercially?
94: Yes. Under the Higgsfield Terms of Use you hold the rights to use your generated content, so API outputs can go into commercial products, advertising, and client work.
95: Can the API generate audio?
96: There are no standalone audio models in the catalog. Some video models, including Seedance, Kling, LTX, and PixVerse, generate native audio inside the clip as a configuration option, which affects the model's rate.
97: Can several people use one API account?
98: Yes. Every account starts as a personal organization, and you can create a team organization and invite people to it. To switch between workspaces, click your profile icon and open Organization. Usage across the account shows up in the Analytics and Billing sections.
99: I lost my API key. Can I see it again?
100: No. The key is visible only at the moment of creation. Generate a new key in the console and update your integration.
101: Do failed generations cost anything?
102: No. Failed requests aren't billed, and the amount is returned to your balance automatically.

200: mermaid-cli
201: This is a command-line interface (CLI) for mermaid. It takes a mermaid definition file as input and generates an SVG/PNG/PDF file as output. There's basic support for converting mermaid code blocks embedded within Markdown files.
202: Installation
203: npm install -g @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli
204: Usage
205: Convert Mermaid mmd Diagram File To SVG
206: mmdc -i input.mmd -o output.svg
207: Note
208: See Alternative installations if you don't want to install the package globally.
209: Locate how to call the mmdc executable for your preferred method
210: i.e. Docker, Yarn, NPM, local install, etc.
211: Examples
212: Create A PNG With A Dark Theme And Transparent Background
213: mmdc -i input.mmd -o output.png -t dark -b transparent
214: Adding custom icon packs to Mermaid
215: mermaid-cli supports two different ways to add custom icon packs to mermaid:
216: Icon packs installed via npm install, e.g. @iconify-json/logos. These can be used via the --iconPacks @iconify-json/logos.
217: Icon packs accessible via URI. These can either be URLs or local file:// URIs to local files. For example, to download the above @iconify-json/logos package from a CDN like jsDelivr, you can do --iconPacksAndUrls logos#https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@iconify-json/logos@1.2.14/icons.json.
218: Animating an SVG file with custom CSS
219: The --cssFile option can be used to inline some custom CSS. It's passed to Mermaid's themeCSS config option.
220: Please see ./test-positive/flowchart1.css for an example of a CSS file that has animations.
221: Warning: Inline CSS files may be blocked by your browser, depending on the HTTP Content-Security-Policy header of the website that hosts your SVG.
222: mmdc --input test-positive/flowchart1.mmd --cssFile test-positive/flowchart1.css -o docs/animated-flowchart.svg
223: Example output: docs/animated-flowchart.svg
224: Selecting the size of the created file
225: The --size value can be used to attempt to create a PNG of the given size,
226: by setting a max-width on the SVG.
227: For narrow diagrams, this would decide set the max height,
228: and for wide diagrams, this will set the max width.
229: For example, the following command will create a PNG of height 4000px:
230: mmdc --input test-positive/flowchart1.mmd --size 4000 -o output.png
231: ![Note]
232: This may not work with all diagram types and/or may require
233: useMaxWidth: true
234: to be set in the diagram's config.
235: Transform a markdown file with mermaid diagrams
236: mmdc -i readme.template.md -o readme.md
237: This command transforms a markdown file itself. The mermaid-cli will find the mermaid diagrams, create SVG files from them and refer to those in the markdown output.
238: This:
239: ### Some markdown
240: ```mermaid
241: graph
242: [....]
243: ```
244: ### Some more markdown
245: ```mermaid
246: sequenceDiagram
247: [....]
248: ```
249: ### Mermaid with custom title/desc
250: ```mermaid
251: graph
252: accTitle: My title here
253: accDescr: My description here
254: A-->B
255: ```
256: Becomes:
257: ### Some markdown
258: ![diagram](./readme-1.svg)
259: ### Some more markdown
260: ![diagram](./readme-2.svg)
261: ### Mermaid with custom title/desc
262: ![My description here](./readme-3.svg "My title here")
263: Piping from stdin
264: You can easily pipe input from stdin. This example shows how to use a heredoc to
265: send a diagram as stdin to mermaid-cli (mmdc).
266: cat << EOF | mmdc --input -
267: graph TD
268: A[Client] --> B[Load Balancer]
269: EOF
270: See All Available Options
271: mmdc -h
272: Alternative installations
273: Use Docker/Podman:
274: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli
275: or pull from Github Container Registry
276: docker pull ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli
277: or e.g. version 8.8.0
278: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli:8.8.0
279: The container looks for input files in /data. So for example, if you have a
280: diagram defined on your system in /path/to/diagrams/diagram.mmd, you can use
281: the container to generate an SVG file as follows:
282: docker run --rm -u `id -u`:`id -g` -v /path/to/diagrams:/data minlag/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
283: Or, if using Podman, instead do:
284: podman run --userns keep-id --user ${UID} --rm -v /path/to/diagrams:/data:z ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
285: The key differences in the podman command versus the docker command are:
286: The addition of the --userns keep-id argument. This allows the container to keep the same UID as the current user's UID in the container namespace instead of mapping to a subuid. To learn more, see the userns=mode documentation.
287: The addition of :z to the end of the volume mapping. This instructs podman to relabel the files in the volume with the SELinux label container_file_t, which allows processes in the container to access the files. See the "Labeling Volume Mounts" section of podman-run (1) for more info.
288: In previous version, the input files were mounted in /home/mermaidcli. You can
289: restore this behaviour with the --workdir option:
290: docker run [...] --workdir=/home/mermaidcli minlag/mermaid-cli [...]
291: Use Node.JS API
292: It's possible to call mermaid-cli via a Node.JS API.
293: Please be aware that the NodeJS API is not covered by semver, as mermaid-cli follows
294: mermaid's versioning.
295: import { run } from "@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli";
296: await run(
297: "input.mmd",
298: "output.svg", // {optional options},
299: );
300: Install locally
301: Some people are having issues
302: installing this tool globally. Installing it locally is an alternative solution:
303: npm install @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli
304: ./node_modules/.bin/mmdc -h
305: Run with npx
306: npx is installed by default with NPM. It
307: downloads and runs commands at the same time. To use Mermaid CLI with npx, you
308: need to use the -p flag because the package name is different than the command
309: it installs (mmdc). npx -p @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli mmdc -h
310: Install with brew
311: Warning
312: This method of installation is no longer supported.
313: For more details, see the discussion.
314: An old version of mermaid-cli can be installed with brew.
315: brew install mermaid-cli
316: Known issues
317: Linux sandbox issue
318: Docker permission denied issue
319: How to setup up mermaid to use already installed chromium?
320: For contributors
321: Contributions are welcome. See the contribution guide.

39: ```
40: <details>
41: <summary>Example output: docs/animated-flowchart.svg</summary>
42: ![docs/animated-flowchart.svg](docs/animated-flowchart.svg)
43: </details>
44: ### Selecting the size of the created file
45: The `--size` value can be used to attempt to create a PNG of the given size,
46: by setting a `max-width` on the SVG.
47: For narrow diagrams, this would decide set the max height,
48: and for wide diagrams, this will set the max width.
49: For example, the following command will create a PNG of height 4000px:
50: ```sh
51: mmdc --input test-positive/flowchart1.mmd --size 4000 -o output.png
52: ```
53: > ![Note]
54: >
55: > This may not work with all diagram types and/or may require
56: > [`useMaxWidth: true`](https://mermaid.js.org/config/schema-docs/config.html#usemaxwidth-1)
57: > to be set in the diagram's config.
58: ### Transform a markdown file with mermaid diagrams
59: ```sh
60: mmdc -i readme.template.md -o readme.md
61: ```
62: This command transforms a markdown file itself. The mermaid-cli will find the mermaid diagrams, create SVG files from them and refer to those in the markdown output.
63: This:
64: ````md
65: ### Some markdown
66: ```mermaid
67: graph
68: [....]
69: ```
70: ### Some more markdown
71: ```mermaid
72: sequenceDiagram
73: [....]
74: ```
75: ### Mermaid with custom title/desc
76: ```mermaid
77: graph
78: accTitle: My title here
79: accDescr: My description here
80: A-->B
81: ```
82: ````
83: Becomes:
84: ```md
85: ### Some markdown
86: ![diagram](./readme-1.svg)
87: ### Some more markdown
88: ![diagram](./readme-2.svg)
89: ### Mermaid with custom title/desc
90: ![My description here](./readme-3.svg "My title here")
91: ```
92: ### Piping from stdin
93: You can easily pipe input from stdin. This example shows how to use a heredoc to
94: send a diagram as stdin to mermaid-cli (mmdc).
95: ```sh
96: cat << EOF | mmdc --input -
97: graph TD
98: A[Client] --> B[Load Balancer]
99: EOF
100: ```
101: ### See All Available Options
102: ```sh
103: mmdc -h
104: ```
105: # Alternative installations
106: ## Use Docker/Podman:
107: ```sh
108: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli
109: ```
110: or pull from Github Container Registry
111: ```sh
112: docker pull ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli
113: ```
114: or e.g. version 8.8.0
115: ```sh
116: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli:8.8.0
117: ```
118: The container looks for input files in `/data`. So for example, if you have a
119: diagram defined on your system in `/path/to/diagrams/diagram.mmd`, you can use
120: the container to generate an SVG file as follows:
121: ```sh
122: docker run --rm -u `id -u`:`id -g` -v /path/to/diagrams:/data minlag/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
123: ```
124: Or, if using [Podman](https://podman.io/), instead do:
125: ```sh
126: podman run --userns keep-id --user ${UID} --rm -v /path/to/diagrams:/data:z ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
127: ```
128: The key differences in the podman command versus the docker command are:
129: - The addition of the `--userns keep-id` argument. This allows the container to keep the same UID as the current user's UID in the container namespace instead of mapping to a subuid. To learn more, see the [`userns=mode` documentation](https://docs.podman.io/en/v4.4/markdown/options/userns.container.html).
130: - The addition of `:z` to the end of the volume mapping. This instructs podman to relabel the files in the volume with the SELinux label `container_file_t`, which allows processes in the container to access the files. See the "Labeling Volume Mounts" section of [podman-run (1)](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html#volume-v-source-volume-host-dir-container-dir-options) for more info.
131: In previous version, the input files were mounted in `/home/mermaidcli`. You can
132: restore this behaviour with the `--workdir` option:
133: ```sh
134: docker run [...] --workdir=/home/mermaidcli minlag/mermaid-cli [...]
135: ```
136: ## Use Node.JS API
137: It's possible to call `mermaid-cli` via a Node.JS API.
138: Please be aware that **the NodeJS API is not covered by semver**, as `mermaid-cli` follows
139: `mermaid`'s versioning.
140: ```js
141: import { run } from "@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli";
142: await run(
143: "input.mmd",
144: "output.svg", // {optional options},
145: );
146: ```
147: ## Install locally
148: Some people are [having issues](https://github.com/mermaidjs/mermaid.cli/issues/15)
149: installing this tool globally. Installing it locally is an alternative solution:
150: ```
151: npm install @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli
152: ./node_modules/.bin/mmdc -h
153: ```
154: ### Run with npx
155: [`npx`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/npx) is installed by default with NPM. It
156: downloads and runs commands at the same time. To use Mermaid CLI with npx, you
157: need to use the `-p` flag because the package name is different than the command
158: it installs (`mmdc`). `npx -p @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli mmdc -h`
159: ## Install with [brew](https://brew.sh)
160: > **Warning**
161: >
162: > This method of installation is no longer supported.
163: > For more details, see the [discussion](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/issues/288).
164: > An old version of mermaid-cli can be installed with brew.
165: >
166: > ```sh
167: > brew install mermaid-cli
168: > ```
169: ## Known issues
170: 1. [Linux sandbox issue](docs/linux-sandbox-issue.md)
171: 2. [Docker permission denied issue](docs/docker-permission-denied.md)
172: 3. [How to setup up mermaid to use already installed chromium?](docs/already-installed-chromium.md)
173: ## For contributors
174: Contributions are welcome. See the [contribution guide](CONTRIBUTING.md).

128: Section titled “YouTube Transcript MCP Server”
129: TranscriptAPI runs a hosted (remote) MCP server at https://transcriptapi.com/mcp. The server uses the same account, API keys, and credits as the REST API.

170: Section titled “What is MCP?”
171: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standardized framework that enables AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT to connect directly with external tools and data sources. With TranscriptAPI’s MCP integration, your AI can fetch YouTube transcripts on-demand without manual copy-pasting or switching between applications.
172: Key Benefits:
173: Direct integration into your AI workflow
174: No manual transcript fetching needed
175: Consistent, structured data format
176: Works with any MCP-compatible platform

178: Section titled “Why Use TranscriptAPI with MCP?”
179: TranscriptAPI offers unique advantages for YouTube Transcript MCP integration:
180: Universal Compatibility
181: Section titled “Universal Compatibility”
182: TranscriptAPI works with any platform that supports MCP. Whether your platform uses OAuth for seamless authentication (like Claude and ChatGPT) or requires manual API key configuration (like OpenAI Agent Builder), we provide both options to ensure maximum compatibility.
183: Proven Reliability
184: Section titled “Proven Reliability”
185: Battle-tested with major AI platforms
186: Consistent performance across all authentication methods
187: Same powerful transcript extraction engine as our REST API
188: Flexible authentication options (OAuth or API Key) based on your platform’s requirements

195: For API Key: An active API key from your dashboard

212: Section titled “Authentication”

214: OAuth (Recommended)

216: OAuth Authentication
217: Section titled “OAuth Authentication”
218: OAuth provides automatic, secure authentication without manual key management. Supported by:
219: Claude (Dynamic Client Registration - optional credentials)
220: ChatGPT (Static Client Registration - requires Client ID/Secret)
221: Any MCP client supporting OAuth 2.1
222: Two Registration Methods:
223: TranscriptAPI supports both Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) and Static Client Registration to work with different platforms:
224: 1. Dynamic Client Registration (Claude, optional)
225: Claude and other clients that support DCR can automatically register
226: No Client ID/Secret needed - just add the MCP server URL
227: The client automatically discovers OAuth endpoints and registers itself
228: You’ll be redirected to authorize access (one-time)
229: 2. Static Client Registration (ChatGPT, required)
230: ChatGPT requires Client ID and Client Secret upfront
231: Get your credentials from the MCP Integration dashboard
232: Expand Advanced: Static OAuth Credentials, click Create New Client, name it, then click Generate Credentials
233: Copy your Client ID and Client Secret
234: In ChatGPT on the web, open Plugins, click the plus button, choose Add custom MCP server, enter the server URL, choose OAuth and paste them in
235: Check I understand and want to continue, click Create as a plugin, install the plugin, then type @ in a new chat to select it
236: How it works:
237: Add the MCP server URL to your client
238: For ChatGPT: Add Client ID and Client Secret
239: For Claude: Credentials are optional (DCR supported)
240: The client automatically discovers our OAuth endpoints
241: You’ll be redirected to authorize access (one-time)
242: Tokens are managed automatically with refresh support
243: Technical Details:
244: Uses OAuth 2.1 with both Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) and Static Registration
245: Authorization server metadata: /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
246: Protected resource metadata: /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
247: Required scope: mcp:access
248: Access tokens prefixed with oat_
249: Benefits:
250: No manual key management (for DCR clients)
251: Automatic token refresh
252: Secure, time-limited access
253: Revocable permissions
254: Platform-specific support (ChatGPT and Claude)
255: API Key Authentication
256: Section titled “API Key Authentication”
257: API Key authentication provides simple, direct access for platforms that don’t support OAuth. Required for:
258: OpenAI Agent Builder
259: Custom MCP implementations
260: Development/testing environments
261: How it works:
262: Get your API key from the API Keys dashboard
263: Add it to your MCP client configuration
264: The key is sent as a Bearer token with each request
265: Configuration: the standard url + headers format for remote MCP servers, used by clients such as Cursor and Windsurf:
266: {
267: "mcpServers": {
268: "transcriptapi": {
269: "url": "https://transcriptapi.com/mcp",
270: "headers": {
271: "Authorization": "Bearer sk_your_api_key_here"
272: }
273: }
274: }
275: }
276: Technical Details:
277: Bearer token authentication: Authorization: Bearer sk_...
278: API keys prefixed with sk_
279: Keys never expire (unless manually revoked)
280: Same key works for both REST API and MCP
281: Security Best Practices:
282: Store keys in environment variables
283: Never commit keys to version control
284: Use separate keys for different environments
285: Rotate keys regularly

331: get_youtube_transcript
332: Section titled “get_youtube_transcript”
333: Extract transcripts from any YouTube video with full control over the output format.
334: Parameters:
335: Parameter
336: Type
337: Default
338: Description
339: video_url
340: string
341: required
342: YouTube video URL or 11-character video ID
343: send_metadata
344: boolean
345: true
346: Include video title, author, and thumbnail
347: format
348: string
349: "text"
350: Output format: "text" (markdown) or "json" (structured)
351: include_timestamp
352: boolean
353: true
354: Include timestamps with each segment
355: language
356: string
357: none
358: Comma-separated priority list, e.g. de,en,asr. Omit for English, or the video’s first available language. asr = auto-generated captions
359: Accepted URL Formats:
360: Full URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ
361: Short URL: https://youtu.be/dQw4w9WgXcQ
362: Video ID only: dQw4w9WgXcQ
363: Example Usage:
364: // Get transcript as markdown with metadata (default)
365: get_youtube_transcript({
366: video_url: "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"
367: })
368: // Returns:
369: {
370: "content": "# Metadata\n## Title: Rick Astley - Never Gonna Give You Up\n## Author: RickAstleyVEVO\n## Author URL: https://www.youtube.com/@RickAstley\n## Thumbnail: https://i.ytimg.com/vi/dQw4w9WgXcQ/hqdefault.jpg\n\n# Transcript\n[0.0s] Never gonna give you up\n[4.12s] Never gonna let you down..."
371: }
372: // Get JSON format without metadata
373: get_youtube_transcript({
374: video_url: "dQw4w9WgXcQ",
375: format: "json",
376: send_metadata: false
377: })
378: // Returns:
379: {
380: "content": {
381: "transcript": [
382: {
383: "text": "Never gonna give you up",
384: "start": 0.0,
385: "duration": 4.12
386: },
387: {
388: "text": "Never gonna let you down",
389: "start": 4.12,
390: "duration": 3.85
391: }
392: ]
393: }
394: }
395: // Get plain text without timestamps
396: get_youtube_transcript({
397: video_url: "dQw4w9WgXcQ",
398: format: "text",
399: include_timestamp: false,
400: send_metadata: false
401: })
402: // Returns:
403: {
404: "content": "# Transcript\nNever gonna give you up Never gonna let you down Never gonna run around and desert you..."
405: }
406: Output Formats:

932: Frequently Asked Questions
933: Section titled “Frequently Asked Questions”
934: What is a YouTube transcript MCP server?
935: It is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that gives an AI assistant a tool for fetching YouTube transcripts. TranscriptAPI’s server is hosted at https://transcriptapi.com/mcp, so the assistant calls it directly and you don’t run anything on your own machine. Besides transcripts, it can search YouTube and list channel and playlist videos.
936: Which AI assistants work with the TranscriptAPI MCP server?
937: Claude and ChatGPT connect with OAuth, and OpenAI Agent Builder connects with an API key. Each has a step-by-step guide: Claude, ChatGPT, OpenAI Agent Builder. Other clients that support remote MCP servers can connect with OAuth 2.1 or an API key sent as a Bearer token. See Supported Clients.
938: Do I need to install or host anything?
939: No. TranscriptAPI hosts the MCP server. You add the server URL in your AI client, then either sign in through OAuth or add your API key.
940: How much does the YouTube MCP server cost?
941: New accounts get 100 free credits with no card required. The get_youtube_video_info and get_channel_latest_videos tools cost no credits. The other tools use 1 credit per call, or 1 credit per page for paginated results. Failed requests don’t use credits. Calls still need a verified email and an account with credits or a plan. Paid plans start at $5 per month for 1,000 credits. See Credit Cost.
942: Is the MCP server the same as the REST API?
943: It uses the same account, API keys, and credits as the TranscriptAPI REST API and the same transcript extraction. You can try a workflow in an AI assistant and later call the REST API from your own code.
944: Can the MCP server get transcripts in other languages?
945: Yes. The get_youtube_video_info tool, which costs no credits, lists the transcript languages a video offers, and get_youtube_transcript accepts a language priority list such as de,en. Codes starting with asr are YouTube’s auto-generated captions.

12: Frequently Asked Questions
13: Q: What applications and platforms support MCP integrations?
14: A: The Model Context Protocol is rapidly gaining adoption where each client supports different MCP features (tools, prompts, resources) depending on their use cases. For the semi-complete list of Clients with feature compatibility details, visit the official MCP clients directory.
15: Q: What Claude plan do I need to use MCP integrations?
16: A: MCP integrations, including the Grain MCP server, are only available on paid Claude plans (Pro, Team, and Enterprise). Free Claude accounts do not support MCP integrations or the ability to connect external tools and data sources. You'll need to upgrade to a paid plan to access the Grain integration and other MCP servers.
17: Q: Are all Grain MCP tools available on every Grain plan?
18: A: Most Grain MCP tools work on all Grain plans (Free, Starter, Business, Enterprise), including meeting search, transcripts, notes, and contact management. However, tools for Deals (list_open_deals, list_all_deals, fetch_deal) and Sales Coaching/Scorecards (list_coaching_feedback, fetch_meeting_coaching_feedback) are restricted to Business and Enterprise plan users only. Free and Starter plan users will receive an error if they attempt to use these premium tools.
19: Q: Is it safe to use MCP servers like Grain's?
20: A: MCP security relies on a trust model, and Grain's MCP server is officially supported by us and aligns with our existing security practices, follows the MCP specification exactly, and uses industry-standard OAuth authentication and HTTPS. All tool usage requires explicit user approval in Claude, and each tool request is scoped to specific data needed for that operation. While no system is 100% secure, Grain's established security practices and transparent approach to data handling make it a safer MCP implementation.
21: Q: How does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) work and what are the privacy implications?
22: A: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that creates a secure bridge between Claude and external services like Grain, where your data stays in your Grain account and is only processed temporarily by Claude to answer questions. As stated by Anthropic, data accessed through MCP integrations is not used to train Claude's models.
23: Q: What data does Grain's MCP server have access to?
24: A: Grain's MCP server only accesses data you already have permission to view in your Grain workspace, including meetings you attended, companies and contacts from those meetings, deal information (with HubSpot integration), and AI-generated notes and transcripts. It has no access to private meetings you weren't invited to or other workspaces you don't belong to. The integration uses OAuth authentication and maintains the same security boundaries as your normal Grain usage.
25: Q: How does Claude verify and approve MCP tool usage?
26: A: Claude requires explicit user approval before using any Grain tool, showing you a dialog with clear descriptions of what each tool will do and offering "use once" or "use for entire session" options. Each tool requires separate approval when first used, and you maintain control over which tools Claude can access in your current session. You can revoke access by starting a new chat session, ensuring that no tools run without your explicit permission.
27: Q: Can I control what data the Grain MCP server shares with Claude?
28: A: Data access is controlled through your existing Grain account permissions, and you can enable/disable specific tools in Claude's integration settings, but you cannot currently exclude specific meetings or companies from MCP access. The integration accesses all data you have permission to see in your Grain workspace and follows your existing permissions rather than providing additional filtering options. Review your Grain workspace permissions before connecting and use targeted prompts to limit the scope of data Claude requests.
29: Q: What is the helpful_usage_information parameter I see in the client's tool responses?
30: A: You may notice the helpful_usage_information parameter appearing in chat interface when the Grain MCP server responds to tool requests. This optional parameter helps Grain's team understand tool usage patterns to improve functionality, and this data is never used as AI training data. 10: Download or export your Grain meetings and transcripts, one at a time, in bulk, or via API.
11: Updated over a month ago
12: Table of contents
13: Whether you're building an AI workflow with your meeting data, migrating to a new tool, or just want your transcripts in a format you can work with elsewhere, Grain gives you several ways to get your data out. The right option depends on how many meetings you need and what you're doing with them.
14: Which option is right for you?
15: What you're trying to do
16: Best option
17: Download one or a few meetings
18: Option 1: Single-meeting download
19: Bulk download transcripts for AI workflows
20: Option 2: Multi-select bulk download
21: Bulk download all meetings in a curated collection
22: Option 3: Playlists bulk export
23: Pipe all workspace meetings to a database or custom AI
24: Option 4: Grain API
25: Query meeting data directly in Claude or ChatGPT
26: Option 5: Grain MCP
27: Option 1: Download a single meeting
28: Use this for one-off downloads when you need a specific meeting's recording or transcript.
29: From the 'Meetings' page:
30: Select the three-dot menu on any meeting card.
31: Select your desired download option:
32: Open in AI: opens your meeting data directly in ChatGPT or Claude.
33: Download transcript for AI: downloads a transcript with metadata for AI.
34: Download recording: downloads an MP4 video of your meeting.
35: Download transcript: downloads the plain transcript text in your desired file format.
36: From inside a meeting:
37: Open the meeting.
38: Click the three-dot icon in the top right.
39: Hover over 'Download' and select your desired download option.
40: Alternatively, inside a meeting, you can:
41: Click the drop-down next to the three-dot icon in the top right.
42: Select your desired download option:
43: Open in AI: opens your meeting data directly in ChatGPT or Claude.
44: Copy/Download transcript for AI: copy or download a transcript with metadata for AI.
45: What you can download
46: Recording — MP4 video file (720p)
47: Transcript — available in Markdown, DOCX, PDF, SRT, or VTT format
48: For more detail on the 'Open in AI' and 'Download transcript for AI' options, including how the transcript is packaged and link expiration, see AI Transcript Actions.
49: Note: Downloading the recording exports the video only. To get the transcript, select 'Download transcript' separately and choose your format.
50: Option 2: Bulk select and download
51: Use this to grab transcripts from multiple meetings at once. Bulk download is limited to 20 meetings at a time.
52: From the 'Meetings' page:
53: On your Meetings page, check the box next to any meeting to enter multi-select mode.
54: Select as many meetings as you want.
55: Choose an action from the bar that appears:
56: Open in AI: combines selected transcripts into a temporary link and opens them in ChatGPT or Claude for analysis.
57: Download: downloads a ZIP file containing Markdown transcripts for all selected meetings.
58: If you've already organized your meetings into a Playlist, you can download all of them without re-selecting:
59: Select the three dots on any Playlist.
60: Use the 'Open in AI' or 'Download' actions available to export your meeting data.
61: Note: The ZIP file contains one Markdown file per meeting. Video recordings are not included.
62: Option 3: Bulk export from a Playlist
63: If you have meetings organized into a Playlist, you can download all transcripts in that Playlist at once, optimized for feeding into an AI tool.
64: 1. Go to 'Playlists' in the left sidebar and open any Playlist.
65: 2. Click the AI actions dropdown arrow at the top of the Playlist.
66: 3. Select 'Download Transcripts for AI'.
67: Grain packages all transcripts in the Playlist into a ZIP folder with a Markdown file for each meeting in the Playlist, ready to paste or upload into any AI tool. See Playlists for more.
68: Option 4: Export via the Grain API
69: Use the API to programmatically extract transcripts and recordings.
70: Personal API token
71: Any user, on every plan including Free, can generate a personal token to access meetings they have permission to view.
72: Go to 'Account settings' → 'Integrations' → 'Personal API'.
73: Click 'Generate personal API token'.
74: Workspace API token (admins only)
75: Workspace admins on Business and Enterprise plans can generate a token with access to all meetings across the workspace.
76: Go to 'Workspace settings' → 'Integrations' → 'API'.
77: Click 'Generate workspace API token'.
78: What you can extract:
79: Transcripts
80: MP4 recordings
81: Rate limit: ~300 API calls per minute.
82: Note: Workspace API tokens provide access to all meetings in your workspace. Only generate one if you're the admin responsible for managing workspace data.
83: For full API reference, see Grain API Documentation
84: Option 5: Use the Grain MCP
85: Use the Grain MCP to query and analyze your meeting data directly inside Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor.
86: What the MCP can access:
87: Meetings and transcripts
88: Notes and action items
89: Coaching feedback
90: Deal data
91: Clips
92: Setup
93: A workspace admin enables the Grain MCP connector for the workspace.
94: Each user connects their own Grain account via OAuth. Users can only access meetings they already have permission to view in Grain.
95: Example prompt:
96: Pull my 10 most recent meeting transcripts and compile them into a single summary. For each meeting, include:
97: - Meeting title and date
98: - Key decisions made
99: - Action items and who owns them
100: Then identify any themes or topics that came up across multiple meetings.
101: Once connected, you can ask your AI tool to pull transcripts, search meeting content, surface action items, or analyze deal data.
102: Note: The MCP doesn't download files, it lets your AI tool read and search meeting data interactively. Use Options 1, 2, or 3 if you need files to keep or move elsewhere. For full setup instructions, see the Official Grain MCP Server.

36: "user_id": "7890-abcd-ef01-2222-3456-7890ffff",
37: "name": "Luke Skywalker",
38: "expires_at": null
39: }

26: Connect AI models to Otter using Model Context Protocol (MCP). Connecting Otter MCP to your AI applications enables secure, scalable access to various language model understandings to power features like smarter summaries, contextual suggestions, and automated insights for all your Otter conversations and meetings.
27: Learn to connect to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Perplexity, or other platforms.
28: What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
29: MCP is an open standard that allows AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT
30: to securely access external data sources. With Otter’s MCP Server, these AI
31: assistants can:
32: ✅ Search your meeting transcripts across all time periods
33: ✅ Analyze patterns and themes across multiple meetings
34: ✅ Generate content using your actual meeting data
35: ✅ Surface insights without leaving your AI workflow
36: 🔑 Key advantage: Your meeting knowledge becomes instantly accessible to AI
37: assistants, eliminating manual copy-paste and context-switching.
38: 🔒 Security: All access is OAuth-authenticated with granular permissions.
39: Your AI assistant can only access meetings you explicitly authorize.
40: Claude setup Learn how to set up Claude
41: Check out Otter.ai in the Claude connectors directory.
42: Connect Otter MCP to Claude.
43: Go to Settings → Connectors → Browse connectors.
44: Note: If your workspace admin has already added Otter.ai, it will appear as an available connector. Click Connect and proceed directly to Step 3.
45: Go to Claude's Otter.ai page and click Connect.
46: Sign in to your Otter account. Review the info and click Authorize access to connect with Claude.
47: Otter MCP is connected to Claude.
48: Enable Otter MCP tool with chat
49: Click on the search and tools menu in the chat box. Toggle on Otter.
50: Configure your Otter MCP tool permissions
51: Claude will prompt for permissions when querying using Otter MCP tools.
52: You can manage permissions for the Otter MCP tool in the connector settings.
53: Under the settings Connectors, click Configure next to Otter or manage through the 3-dot menu.
54: Manage each of the tools' permissions. We recommend setting it to Always allow.
55: ChatGPT setup Learn how to set up ChatGPT
56: Connect Otter MCP to ChatGPT. Otter.ai is available in the ChatGPT App Store.
57: Check out Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.
58: Sign in to the ChatGPT web version. Go to Settings.
59: Note: To connect to Otter MCP, you must currently complete the connection through the web version of Otter. Connecting directly through the desktop app is not yet supported. Once the connection is established on the web, it will automatically be available in the desktop app.
60: Go to Apps and add apps. The option may vary depending on your existing account.
61: Go to Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.
62: Click Connect.
63: Carefully review the information and click Connect Otter.ai.
64: Sign in to your Otter.ai account. Carefully review the information and click Authorize access to proceed.
65: Otter.ai is now connected to your ChatGPT account.
66: Enable Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT. Now that Otter is connected, you can work from the ChatGPT web browser or the desktop app.
67: Click the + (plus icon). Click ••• More and select Otter.ai.
68: Type @ and select Otter.ai.
69: When starting a new chat, make sure Otter.ai is showing. If you do not see otter.ai, select it again through the steps above.
70: Using Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT
71: Otter uses 3 tools in ChatGPT to query your meetings:
72: fetch
73: get user info
74: search
75: If prompted, accept the tool request to proceed.
76: You can click any source to go directly to the Otter conversation.
77: If you are experiencing any issues querying your Otter conversations, we recommend specifically mentioning the Otter tool you want to use in your query.
78: Manage Otter MCP settings for ChatGPT in Apps.
79: Cursor setup Learn how to set up Cursor
80: Connect Otter MCP to Cursor. Refer to Cursor’s documentation on connecting MCP servers for more info.
81: Navigate to Cursor settings. Click Tools & MCP. Click Add Custom MCP.
82: Configure the JSON file with the following. Save changes to the file.
83: {
84: "mcpServers": {
85: "otter_meeting_mcp": {
86: "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
87: }
88: }
89: }
90: Navigate back to Tools & MCP. Click Connect.
91: Click Open.
92: Sign in to your Otter account. Click Authorize access.
93: Otter MCP is connected to Cursor.
94: Enable Cursor
95: Enable Otter MCP by ensuring it's toggled ON under Cursor Tools & MCP settings and tools enabled. Cursor will automatically use available tools.
96: If a tool is disabled, click on the grayed-out tool to re-enable.
97: Perplexity Learn how to set up Perplexity
98: Connect Otter MCP to Perplexity using custom connectors to securely access and reference your Otter conversations, meeting notes, and AI insights directly within Perplexity.
99: Note: Perplexity’s UI may change over time. Refer to Perplexity’s documentation for the latest instructions on connecting a custom connector.
100: Navigate to the Connectors settings page. The location may vary depending on whether you are using an individual or an Enterprise account.
101: Click + Custom connector.
102: Configure using the following settings and click Add.
103: Name: Otter.ai
104: Description: Meetings from Otter
105: MCP server URL: https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp
106: Icon: The Otter icon can be downloaded here.
107: Sign in to your Otter account and click Authorize access.
108: Otter MCP is connected to Perplexity.
109: Enable Perplexity
110: Make sure the connector is enabled before submitting your query. You may need to grant permissions the first time you use the provided tools.
111: Connect Otter MCP to other AI tools You may be able to connect Otter MCP to your AI tool depending on your platform
112: Otter MCP can be connected to third-party AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP) using a JSON configuration file. Setup varies by platform and is managed entirely within your AI tool’s configuration. Configuration, behavior, and support depend on the specific platform you are using. Refer to your tool's documentation to connect to an MCP server.
113: Before you begin
114: Your AI tool must support MCP
115: You should be familiar with editing JSON configuration files
116: OAuth authentication is still required to connect
117: JSON Configuration file
118: {
119: "mcpServers": {
120: "otter": {
121: "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
122: }
123: }
124: }
125: Complete setup in your AI tool
126: Add a custom MCP and configure the JSON file with the above.
127: Connect and authenticate with your Otter account.
128: Verify the Otter MCP server appears, and tools are available.
129: Note: We’ll continue adding step-by-step guides for more AI tools. In the meantime, setup may vary by platform and is completed at your discretion.

131: Name

154: Pull all meetings in Q3 discussing sales initiatives and the top ideas.

158: Onboarding Acceleration

166: Meeting Prep Intelligence

168: FAQs
169: Is Otter MCP available for all AI applications?
170: We are working to release Otter MCP for all AI applications. Contact our Otter Support Team for help setting up Otter MCP with your AI application.
171: Note: Google Gemini's support for MCP tools is not yet available, according to this thread; however, Gemini's command line interface (CLI) does support connecting to MCPs. Refer to Google's documentation for the most up-to-date information.

178: You can access all meetings that you have captured in Otter, as well as any meetings shared with you from other users in your Workspace.

132: > ```
133: ## Get next 10 meetings
134: Use the `next_cursor` from the previous response to get the next page of meetings.
135: ```cURL bash theme={null}
136: curl https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/meetings \
137: -H "X-Api-Key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
138: -d cursor=CURSOR_FROM_PREVIOUS_RESPONSE
139: ```
140: ```Python python theme={null}
141: import requests
142: cursor = "CURSOR_FROM_PREVIOUS_RESPONSE"
143: response = requests.get(
144: f"https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/meetings?cursor={cursor}",
145: headers={"X-Api-Key": "YOUR_API_KEY"}
146: )
147: ```
148: ```Typescript TypeScript theme={null}
149: const cursor = "CURSOR_FROM_PREVIOUS_RESPONSE";
150: const response = await fetch(`https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/meetings?cursor=${cursor}`, {
151: headers: {"X-Api-Key": "YOUR_API_KEY"}
152: });
153: ```
154: > [!NOTE]
155: >
156: > If you're using our [TypeScript or Python SDKs](https://developers.fathom.ai/sdks.md), pagination is handled automatically - no need to manage cursors manually. See [SDK Pagination](https://developers.fathom.ai/sdks/pagination.md) for examples.
157: ## Find specific meetings and get their transcripts
158: Let's say you met with `john.doe@client.com` a couple times during August and want to pull those transcripts. Use filters to return just those meetings.
159: ```cURL cURL theme={null}
160: curl https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/meetings \
161: -H "X-Api-Key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
162: -d include_transcript=true \
163: -d recorded_by[]=me@mydomain.com \
164: -d created_after=2024-08-01T00:00:00Z \
165: -d created_before=2024-09-01T00:00:00Z
166: # include_transcript=true: get transcripts in the response
167: # recorded_by[]=me@mydomain.com: meetings you recorded
168: # created_after/before: August date range
169: ```
170: ```Python Python theme={null}
171: import requests
172: response = requests.get(
173: "https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/meetings",
174: headers={"X-Api-Key": "YOUR_API_KEY"},
175: params={
176: "include_transcript": "true", # get transcripts in the response
177: "recorded_by[]": "me@mydomain.com", # meetings you recorded
178: "created_after": "2024-08-01T00:00:00Z", # August 1st onward
179: "created_before": "2024-09-01T00:00:00Z" # before September 1st
180: }
181: )
182: meetings = response.json()["items"]
183: transcript = meetings[0]["transcript"] # Get first meeting's transcript
184: ```
185: ```Typescript TypeScript theme={null}
186: const params = new URLSearchParams({
187: include_transcript: "true", // get transcripts in the response
188: "recorded_by[]": "me@mydomain.com", // meetings you recorded
189: created_after: "2024-08-01T00:00:00Z", // August 1st onward
190: created_before: "2024-09-01T00:00:00Z" // before September 1st
191: });
192: const response = await fetch(`https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/meetings?${params}`, {
193: headers: {"X-Api-Key": "YOUR_API_KEY"}
194: });
195: const meetings = await response.json();
196: const transcript = meetings.items[0].transcript; // Get first meeting's transcript
197: ```
198: > [!NOTE]
199: >
200: > You can also fetch transcripts separately using the [/recordings/{recording_id}/transcript](https://developers.fathom.ai/api-reference/recordings/get-transcript.md) endpoint. **OAuth apps** must use this approach since they can't use `include_transcript` or `include_summary`.
201: ## Next steps
202: Now that you you've made your first API calls, time to go deeper:
203: > [card] [API documentation](https://developers.fathom.ai/api-overview.md)
204: >
205: > See all available endpoints and methods

208: > Set up a webhook

211: > Use our Typescript or Python SDK

213: >
214: > Build a Fathom integration with OAuth

4: # Building with OAuth
5: > Launching an integration for mutual customers with Fathom? Let's get started!
6: ## Integrating your app with Fathom
7: If you're developing a public app that you wish to integrate with Fathom, you should build it using OAuth.
8: OAuth apps are eligible for promotion by Fathom and can unlock visibility in our App Marketplace, as well as co-marketing opportunities. They are subject to review to ensure the best experience for all users.
9: ## How to launch your app:
10: ### 👀 Step 1: Check out Fathom’s partner enablement resources
11: Learn more about our product and scope out your integration opportunities:
12: * [Fathom Partner Demo Walkthrough](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1WKr6TWp01pxijE9OFjYsqVEseS3-ZcCJ/view)
13: * [Fathom’s Upcoming Webinars and Recordings](https://watch.getcontrast.io/fathom-ai)

16: >
17: > Configure your redirects and receive your OAuth credentials. (2 mins)
18: ### 🔑 Step 3: Configure OAuth Authentication
19: Once you have your OAuth credentials, [set up authentication](https://developers.fathom.ai/sdks/oauth.md) using our SDK.

24: Reach out to [help@fathom.video](mailto:help@fathom.video) if you have any questions or need support on launch materials (ex: information for an integration listing on your site, amplification of a social post, etc.)

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://developers.fathom.ai/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # OAuth
5: > Use OAuth authentication with the Fathom SDKs
6: ## OAuth Authentication
7: > [!NOTE]
8: >
9: > OAuth users need to register an app with us before using this feature. Visit our [OAuth Setup Guide](https://developers.fathom.ai/oauth.md) to get your client credentials and configure your redirect URL.
10: Both TypeScript and Python SDKs support OAuth 2.0 authentication for building integrations that can be installed by multiple Fathom accounts.
11: ***
12: ### Step 1: Get Authorization URL
13: Using the `Client ID` and `Client Secret` you received when registering your app, generate an authorization URL that users will visit to grant your app access:
14: ```typescript TypeScript theme={null}
15: import { Fathom } from 'fathom-typescript';
16: const url = Fathom.getAuthorizationUrl({
17: clientId: 'YOUR_CLIENT_ID',
18: clientSecret: 'YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET',
19: redirectUri: 'https://your_redirect_url',
20: scope: 'public_api',
21: state: 'randomState123',
22: });
23: // Redirect user to this URL
24: console.log(url);
25: ```
26: ```python Python theme={null}
27: from fathom_python import Fathom
28: url = Fathom.get_authorization_url(
29: "YOUR_CLIENT_ID", # client ID
30: "your_redirect_url",
31: "public_api", # required scope
32: "randomState123"
33: )
34: print(url)
35: ```
36: ### Step 2: Handle OAuth Callback
37: After the user authorizes your app, they'll be redirected back to your redirect URI with an authorization code. Use this code to exchange it for access tokens:
38: ```typescript TypeScript theme={null}
39: import { Fathom } from 'fathom-typescript';
40: // User gets redirected here with code
41: const tokenStore = Fathom.newTokenStore(); // demo only — use persistent store in production
42: const fathom = new Fathom({
43: security: Fathom.withAuthorization({
44: clientId: "YOUR_CLIENT_ID",
45: clientSecret: "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET",
46: code: "AUTHORIZATION_CODE_FROM_CALLBACK",
47: redirectUri: "https://your_redirect_url",
48: tokenStore
49: }),
50: });
51: // Now you can make requests and the SDK will refresh tokens as needed
52: const result = await fathom.listMeetings({});
53: ```
54: ```python Python theme={null}
55: from fathom_python import Fathom
56: # User gets redirected back to your redirect URI with a code
57: token_store = Fathom.new_token_store() # demo only — use persistent store in production
58: fathom = Fathom(security=Fathom.with_authorization(
59: "YOUR_CLIENT_ID", # client_id
60: "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET", # client_secret
61: "AUTHORIZATION_CODE_FROM_CALLBACK", # code
62: "your_redirect_uri",
63: token_store
64: ))
65: result = fathom.list_meetings()
66: print(result)
67: ```
68: > [!NOTE]
69: >
70: > newTokenStore() is an in-memory store — great for demos and quick starts. For production, you'll want a persistent TokenStore so users only need to install once.
71: ### Step 3: Token Management & Persistence
72: For production, you'll want to implement your own `TokenStore` that persists tokens to a database, cache, or file.
73: The SDK will automatically call your `set()` when new tokens are issued, and `get()` when it needs to reuse or refresh them.
74: #### Example: Python persistent store (SQLite)
75: > [!NOTE]
76: >
77: > This SQLite example is meant as a simple demo. In production, you’ll want to plug in whatever storage makes sense for your stack (e.g. Postgres, Redis, cloud secret store).
78: ```python theme={null}
79: import sqlite3
80: from fathom_python import Fathom
81: class SQLiteTokenStore(Fathom.TokenStore):
82: def __init__(self, db_path="tokens.db"):
83: self.db_path = db_path
84: self._init_db()
85: def _init_db(self):
86: conn = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path)
87: conn.execute("""
88: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fathom_tokens (
89: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
90: token TEXT,
91: refresh_token TEXT,
92: expires INTEGER
93: )
94: """)
95: conn.commit()
96: conn.close()
97: def get(self):
98: conn = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path)
99: row = conn.execute("SELECT token, refresh_token, expires FROM fathom_tokens WHERE id = 1").fetchone()
100: conn.close()
101: return {"token": row[0], "refresh_token": row[1], "expires": row[2]} if row else None
102: def set(self, token, refresh_token, expires):
103: conn = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path)
104: conn.execute("""
105: INSERT INTO fathom_tokens (id, token, refresh_token, expires)
106: VALUES (1, ?, ?, ?)
107: ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET token=excluded.token,
108: refresh_token=excluded.refresh_token,
109: expires=excluded.expires
110: """, (token, refresh_token, expires))
111: conn.commit()
112: conn.close()
113: ```
114: **Usage:**
115: ```python theme={null}
116: token_store = SQLiteTokenStore()
117: fathom = Fathom(security=Fathom.with_authorization(
118: client_id,
119: client_secret,
120: authorization_code,
121: redirect_uri,
122: token_store
123: ))
124: ```
125: #### Further examples
126: For a real-world production example, see [how Pylon implemented OAuth and token storage](https://developers.fathom.ai/inspiration/pylon.md) as part of their Fathom integration.
127: ### Common Mistakes
128: * **Calling `tokenStore.get()` too early**
129: Nothing will be there yet — tokens are only written after the SDK exchanges the authorization code.
130: * **Assuming tokens never expire**
131: Access tokens are short-lived. Always persist the refresh token and let the SDK refresh automatically.
132: * **Using `newTokenStore()` in production**
133: It’s an in-memory store for demos only. Use a persistent store (database, Redis, file, etc.) so tokens survive restarts.
134: ### Manual Token Exchange (Optional)
135: If you prefer to handle the token exchange yourself (or to debug), you can call the OAuth token endpoint directly.
136: > [!NOTE]
137: >
138: > The SDK handles token exchange and refresh automatically. You only need this section if you’re debugging or implementing your own flow.
139: **Exchange authorization code for tokens:**
140: ```bash theme={null}
141: curl -X POST https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/oauth2/token \
142: -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
143: -d "grant_type=authorization_code" \
144: -d "code=AUTH_CODE" \
145: -d "client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID" \
146: -d "client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET" \
147: -d "redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URI"
148: ```
149: This returns a JSON object with both an `access_token` and a `refresh_token`.
150: **Refresh an expired access token:**
151: ```bash theme={null}
152: curl -X POST https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/oauth2/token \
153: -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
154: -d "grant_type=refresh_token" \
155: -d "refresh_token=YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN" \
156: -d "client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID" \
157: -d "client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"
158: ```
159: This also returns a JSON object with both an `access_token` and a `refresh_token`. Use the new `access_token` in API requests. Store and use the new `refresh_token` the next time your access token expires. A `refresh_token` can only be used once. If it is unused, it stays valid until the user revokes access.
160: ### OAuth Handler Examples
161: Complete OAuth flow implementations for web frameworks:
162: ```typescript Express.js theme={null}
163: import express from 'express';
164: import { Fathom } from 'fathom-typescript';
165: const app = express();
166: // OAuth initiation endpoint
167: app.get('/auth/fathom', (req, res) => {
168: const authUrl = Fathom.getAuthorizationUrl({
169: clientId: process.env.FATHOM_CLIENT_ID!,
170: clientSecret: process.env.FATHOM_CLIENT_SECRET!,
171: redirectUri: 'https://your-app.com/auth/fathom/callback',
172: scope: 'public_api',
173: state: 'random_state_string',
174: });
175: res.redirect(authUrl);
176: });
177: // OAuth callback endpoint
178: app.get('/auth/fathom/callback', async (req, res) => {
179: const { code, state } = req.query;
180: if (!code || typeof code !== 'string') {
181: return res.status(400).send('Authorization code required');
182: }
183: try {
184: const tokenStore = Fathom.newTokenStore();
185: const fathom = new Fathom({
186: security: Fathom.withAuthorization({
187: clientId: process.env.FATHOM_CLIENT_ID!,
188: clientSecret: process.env.FATHOM_CLIENT_SECRET!,
189: code,
190: redirectUri: 'https://your-app.com/auth/fathom/callback',
191: tokenStore
192: }),
193: });
194: // Test the connection
195: const meetings = await fathom.listMeetings({});
196: res.json({ success: true, meetingsCount: meetings.items?.length || 0 });
197: } catch (error) {
198: console.error('OAuth error:', error);
199: res.status(500).send('OAuth authentication failed');
200: }
201: });
202: app.listen(3000, () => {
203: console.log('Server running on port 3000');
204: });
205: ```
206: ```python Flask theme={null}
207: from flask import Flask, request, redirect, jsonify
208: from fathom_python import Fathom
209: import os
210: app = Flask(__name__)
211: # OAuth initiation endpoint
212: @app.route('/auth/fathom')
213: def auth_fathom():
214: auth_url = Fathom.get_authorization_url(
215: os.getenv('FATHOM_CLIENT_ID'),
216: 'https://your-app.com/auth/fathom/callback',
217: 'public_api',
218: 'random_state_string'
219: )
220: return redirect(auth_url)
221: # OAuth callback endpoint
222: @app.route('/auth/fathom/callback')
223: def auth_fathom_callback():
224: code = request.args.get('code')
225: state = request.args.get('state')
226: if not code:
227: return 'Authorization code required', 400
228: try:
229: token_store = Fathom.new_token_store()
230: fathom = Fathom(security=Fathom.with_authorization(
231: os.getenv('FATHOM_CLIENT_ID'),
232: os.getenv('FATHOM_CLIENT_SECRET'),
233: code,
234: 'https://your-app.com/auth/fathom/callback',
235: token_store
236: ))
237: # Test the connection
238: meetings = fathom.list_meetings()
239: return jsonify({
240: 'success': True,
241: 'meetingsCount': len(meetings.items) if meetings.items else 0
242: })
243: except Exception as e:
244: print(f'OAuth error: {e}')
245: return 'OAuth authentication failed', 500
246: if __name__ == '__main__':
247: app.run(port=3000)
248: ```
249: ### OAuth Scopes
250: Currently, the only available scope is:
251: * `public_api` — Access to the Fathom API
252: ### OAuth Rate limits
253: 60 requests per 60 seconds per OAuth app for the `https://api.fathom.ai/external/v1/oauth2/token` endpoint

4: # Get started with Consensus API
5: > Search over 400 million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, with the Consensus REST API.
6: The Consensus API lets you search 400+ million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, over a single REST endpoint. Send a query and get back ranked papers with titles, authors, journals, publication years, citation counts, and direct links.
7: ## Quickstart
8: Make your first API call in a few minutes. Every plan includes API access, and the Free plan includes 30 calls a month.
9: **1. Sign in to Consensus**
10: Create a free account or sign in at [consensus.app](https://consensus.app). The dashboard in the next step only opens when you're signed in.
11: **2. Open the API & MCP Dashboard**
12: Go to [consensus.app/api-mcp](https://consensus.app/api-mcp/). You can also get there from your profile icon: choose **API & MCP Dashboard**.
13: **3. Create and copy an API key**
14: Click **Create API key**, name the key, and click **Copy API key**. The full key is shown only once, so store it somewhere safe.
15: Already have a key? Open **Keys and clients** and click **New key**.
16: **4. Make your first request**

19: export CONSENSUS_API_KEY="paste-your-key-here"

21: Then search. `query` is the only required parameter, and the key goes in the `x-api-key` header.

34: resp.raise_for_status()
