1: ---
2: title: "Reducto API Reference for Coding Agents"
3: description: "Compact reference for AI coding agents integrating Reducto"
4: ---
5: > Documentation Index
6: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.reducto.ai/llms.txt
7: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
8: # Reducto API Reference for Coding Agents
9: A compact reference for AI coding agents. Every Parse example uses [r-1](/parse/r-1). Keep it that way: set `settings.model` to `"r-1"` and add no other parse options unless the task needs them.
10: ## Fastest path
11: | Situation | Use | First call |
12: |---|---|---|
13: | Local file or folder in an agent workspace | [CLI](/cli) | `reducto parse ./document.pdf` |
14: | Agent calls Reducto as tools | [MCP server](/mcp-server) | `parse_document(document_url="https://cdn.reducto.ai/samples/fidelity-example.pdf")` |
15: | Python app | Python SDK | `client.parse.run(input=url, settings={"model": "r-1"})` |
16: | Node.js app | Node.js SDK | `await client.parse.run({ input: url, settings: { model: "r-1" } })` |
17: | No SDK | REST | `POST https://platform.reducto.ai/parse` |
18: ## Authentication
19: Create an API key in [Studio](https://studio.reducto.ai/) under **API Keys** and export it:
20: ```bash
21: export REDUCTO_API_KEY="your_api_key_here"
22: ```
23: The Python, Node.js, and Go SDKs read `REDUCTO_API_KEY` from the environment.
24: ## Which endpoint
25: | I want to... | Endpoint | Key input |
26: |---|---|---|
27: | Get all text, tables, and figures as chunks with bounding boxes | `/parse` | `settings.model: "r-1"` |
28: | Pull specific fields into JSON | `/extract` | `instructions.schema` |
29: | Split a document into named sections by page | `/split` | `split_description` |
30: | Classify a document's type | `/classify` | `classification_schema` |
31: | Fill PDF or DOCX forms | `/edit` | `document_url`, `edit_instructions` |
32: | Upload a local file | `/upload` | multipart `file` |
33: | Run in the background | `/parse_async`, `/extract_async`, `/split_async`, `/classify_async`, `/edit_async` | `webhook` |
34: | Get a job's status or result | `GET /job/{job_id}` | - |
35: Supported inputs: PDF, images, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, CSV, and [30+ other formats](/upload/overview). Upload up to 100MB directly or 5GB with a [presigned URL](/upload/large-files).
36: ## Quick start (Python)
37: ```python
38: from pathlib import Path
39: import requests
40: from reducto import Reducto
41: client = Reducto()
42: upload = client.upload(file=Path("document.pdf"))
43: parse = client.parse.run(input=upload.file_id, settings={"model": "r-1"})
44: chunks = (
45: requests.get(parse.result.url).json()
46: if parse.result.type == "url"
47: else parse.result.chunks
48: )
49: extract = client.extract.run(
50: input=upload.file_id,
51: instructions={"schema": {
52: "type": "object",
53: "properties": {"total": {"type": "number", "description": "Invoice total"}},
54: }},
55: parsing={"settings": {"model": "r-1"}},
56: )
57: print(extract.result[0])
58: split = client.split.run(
59: input=upload.file_id,
60: split_description=[{"name": "Summary", "description": "Executive summary pages"}],
61: parsing={"settings": {"model": "r-1"}},
62: )
63: ```
64: Edit takes `document_url`, not `input`.
65: ## Parse parameters
66: `POST /parse`. Only `input` and `settings.model` are needed.
67: | Parameter | Default | Description |
68: |---|---|---|
69: | `input` | required | `reducto://` file ID, URL, presigned URL, or `jobid://` |
70: | `settings.model` | account default | Set to `"r-1"`. |
71: | `retrieval.chunking.chunk_mode` | `"disabled"` | `disabled` (one chunk), `variable` (best for RAG), `section`, `page`, `block`, `page_sections` |
72: | `retrieval.chunking.chunk_size` | `null` | Target characters per chunk |
73: | `retrieval.filter_blocks` | `[]` | Block types to drop from `content` and `embed`, such as `"Header"`, `"Footer"`, `"Page Number"` |
74: | `formatting.table_output_format` | `"dynamic"` | `dynamic`, `html`, `md`, `json`, `csv` |
75: | `formatting.add_page_markers` | `false` | Add page markers to the output |
76: | `formatting.merge_tables` | `false` | Merge consecutive tables with the same columns |
77: | `settings.page_range` | `null` | `{"start": 1, "end": 10}`, 1-indexed |
78: | `settings.return_images` | `[]` | `"figure"`, `"table"`, `"page"` |
79: | `settings.document_password` | `null` | Password for encrypted files |
80: | `settings.persist_results` | `false` | Keep results past 24 hours |
81: | `settings.force_url_result` | `false` | Always return a URL result |
82: | `settings.timeout` | `null` | Timeout in seconds |
83: Optional add-ons:
84: | Parameter | Description |
85: |---|---|
86: | `settings.return_citations` | Word-level boxes in `block.extra.word_citations`, and cell boxes for tables in `extra.cell_citations`. Not with `merge_tables`. |
87: | `enhance.advanced_chart_agent` | Structured series data for charts. Adds latency. |
88: | `enhance.agentic` with `prompt` | LLM enrichment. Not recommended: adds latency and can lower accuracy. |
89: Starting December 7, 2026, Parse defaults to r-1. To keep legacy Parse, set `settings.model` to `"legacy"`. Do not use `settings.ocr_system`, `settings.extraction_mode`, `enhance.summarize_figures`, `enhance.intelligent_ordering`, or agentic entries without a prompt. They only apply to [legacy Parse](/configs/parse/legacy).
90: ### Parse response shape
91: ```json
92: {
93: "job_id": "uuid",
94: "result": {
95: "type": "full",
96: "chunks": [{
97: "content": "# Heading\n\nText...",
98: "embed": "Heading. Text...",
99: "blocks": [{
100: "type": "Title",
101: "content": "Heading",
102: "bbox": {"left": 0.1, "top": 0.05, "width": 0.3, "height": 0.04, "page": 1},
103: "confidence": "high"
104: }]
105: }]
106: },
107: "usage": {"num_pages": 3, "credits": 4.0},
108: "studio_link": "https://studio.reducto.ai/job/..."
109: }
110: ```
111: When `result.type` is `"url"`, fetch the chunks from `result.url`. They are plain dicts.
112: ## Extract Parameters
113: `POST /extract`. Pull specific fields from documents into structured JSON using a schema.
114: Extract runs Parse internally. If a value doesn't appear in the Parse output, Extract cannot extract it.
115: | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
116: |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
117: | `input` | string \| string[] | **required** | File ID, URL, `jobid://...`, or array of job IDs to combine |
118: | `instructions.schema` | object | `{}` | JSON Schema defining fields to extract. Field names and descriptions directly influence accuracy. |
119: | `instructions.system_prompt` | string | `"Be precise and thorough."` | Document-level context for the LLM |
120: | `settings.array_extract` | bool | `false` | **Deprecated.** Use `settings.deep_extract` instead. |
121: | `settings.deep_extract` | bool | `false` | Agentic mode that iteratively refines output for near-perfect accuracy. Preferred for complex or long (array-heavy) extractions. Higher cost/latency. |
122: | `settings.citations.enabled` | bool | `false` | Return source page, bbox, and text for each value. **Mutually exclusive with chunking.** |
123: | `settings.citations.numerical_confidence` | bool | `true` | Include 0-1 confidence scores (vs "high"/"low") |
124: | `settings.include_images` | bool | `false` | Include page images in extraction context |
125: | `settings.optimize_for_latency` | bool | `false` | Higher priority processing at 2x cost |
126: | `parsing` | object | `{}` | Parse options. Set `parsing.settings.model` to `"r-1"`. Ignored if input is `jobid://`. |
127: ### Extract Response Shape
128: ```json
129: {
130: "result": [
131: {
132: "invoice_number": "INV-2024-001",
133: "total": 1250.00,
134: "line_items": [{"description": "Widget", "amount": 500.00}]
135: }
136: ],
137: "job_id": "uuid",
138: "usage": {"num_fields": 4, "num_pages": 2, "credits": 10.0},
139: "studio_link": "https://studio.reducto.ai/job/..."
140: }
141: ```
142: With `citations.enabled: true`, each value is wrapped:
143: ```json
144: {
145: "result": {
146: "total": {
147: "value": 1250.00,
148: "citations": [
149: {
150: "type": "Table",
151: "content": "Total: $1,250.00",
152: "bbox": {"left": 0.04, "top": 0.26, "width": 0.45, "height": 0.50, "page": 2},
153: "confidence": "high"
154: }
155: ]
156: }
157: }
158: }
159: ```
160: ---
161: ## Split Parameters
162: `POST /split`. Divide documents into named sections by page number.
163: Split runs Parse internally, then uses an LLM to classify pages against your section descriptions.
164: | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
165: |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
166: | `input` | string | **required** | File ID, URL, or `jobid://...` |
167: | `split_description` | array | **required** | List of `{"name": "...", "description": "..."}` section definitions |
168: | `split_rules` | string | `"Split the document into the applicable sections..."` | Natural language rules for splitting behavior |
169: | `settings.table_cutoff` | `"truncate"` \| `"preserve"` | `"truncate"` | `truncate`: first rows only (faster). `preserve`: all content. |
170: | `parsing` | object | `{}` | Parse options. Set `parsing.settings.model` to `"r-1"`. Ignored if input is `jobid://`. |
171: ### Split Response Shape
172: ```json
173: {
174: "result": {
175: "splits": [
176: {"name": "Executive Summary", "pages": [1, 2]},
177: {"name": "Financial Statements", "pages": [3, 4, 5, 6]},
178: {"name": "Risk Factors", "pages": [7, 8, 9]}
179: ]
180: },
181: "job_id": "uuid",
182: "usage": {"num_pages": 9, "credits": 6.0}
183: }
184: ```
185: ---
186: ## Edit Parameters
187: `POST /edit`. Fill PDF forms and modify DOCX documents.
188: **Note:** Edit uses `document_url` as its input parameter, not `input` like other endpoints.
189: | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
190: |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
191: | `document_url` | string | **required** | File ID or URL of the document to edit (this is `document_url`, not `input`) |
192: | `edit_instructions` | string | **required** | Natural language instructions. Be explicit: `"Fill Name: John Doe, Date: 2024-01-15"` |
193: | `edit_options.color` | string | `"#FF0000"` | Highlight color for edits (DOCX only) |
194: | `edit_options.enable_overflow_pages` | bool | `false` | Create appendix pages for text exceeding field capacity (PDF only) |
195: | `form_schema` | array \| null | `null` | Pre-defined field locations for repeatable form filling. Skips detection. |
196: ### Edit Response Shape
197: ```json
198: {
199: "document_url": "https://storage.reducto.ai/filled-form.pdf?...",
200: "form_schema": [
201: {
202: "bbox": {"left": 0.1, "top": 0.2, "width": 0.4, "height": 0.03, "page": 1},
203: "description": "Name field",
204: "type": "text",
205: "value": "John Doe",
206: "filled": true
207: }
208: ],
209: "usage": {"num_pages": 2, "credits": 8},
210: "warnings": null
211: }
212: ```
213: The `document_url` is a presigned URL valid for 24 hours. Save the returned `form_schema` to reuse for the same form type (skips field detection). Each field's `value` is the value Edit wrote and `filled` is `true` if Edit wrote it. Set `value` to `null` before reuse, or the old value becomes a fixed value. `warnings` lists problems such as "no form fields were filled", or is `null`.
214: ---
215: ## Classify Parameters
216: `POST /classify`. Categorize a document before processing.
217: | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
218: |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
219: | `input` | string | **required** | File ID or URL |
220: | `classification_schema` | array | **required** | List of `{"category": "...", "criteria": ["...", "..."]}` |
221: | `page_range` | object \| null | `null` | Pages to use for classification context. Defaults to first 5 pages. Max 10 pages. |
222: | `document_metadata` | string \| null | `null` | Optional metadata to include in classification prompt |
223: ### Classify Response Shape
224: ```json
225: {
226: "result": {
227: "category": "invoice"
228: },
229: "job_id": "uuid",
230: "duration": 1.23
231: }
232: ```
233: ---
234: ## Async Processing
235: Parse, Extract, Split, Classify, and Edit have async variants (`/parse_async`, `/extract_async`, `/split_async`, `/classify_async`, `/edit_async`). Async endpoints return a `job_id` immediately and process in the background. Poll `GET /job/{job_id}` for the result.
236: ```python
237: # Submit async job
238: job = client.parse.run_job(input=upload.file_id, settings={"model": "r-1"})
239: print(job.job_id)
240: # Poll for results
241: import time
242: while True:
243: result = client.job.get(job.job_id)
244: if result.status in ("Completed", "Failed"):
245: break
246: time.sleep(2)
247: ```
248: Configure webhooks for push-based delivery instead of polling.
249: ---
250: ## Error Codes
251: | HTTP Status | Meaning | Common cause |
252: |-------------|---------|--------------|
253: | 401 | Unauthorized | Missing or invalid `REDUCTO_API_KEY` |
254: | 422 | Validation error | Invalid parameters, schema too large, or constraint violation |
255: | 429 | Rate limited | Too many concurrent requests. Retry with backoff. |
256: | 500 | Server error | Transient issue. Retry with backoff. |
257: ---
258: ## Useful Links
259: - [API Reference](/api-reference/api/sections/parse/operations/parse): Full OpenAPI spec with request/response details
260: - [Parse Configuration](/configs/overview): All configuration options
261: - [Cookbooks](/cookbooks/overview): End-to-end tutorials (invoice extraction, form filling, RAG)
262: - [Error Codes](/reference/error-codes): Complete error catalog
263: - [Checking API Health & Usage](/reference/checking-api-health): Hosted API availability, usage data, and throttling signals
264: - [Rate Limits](/reference/rate-limits): Request limits and quotas
265: - [Credit Usage](/reference/credit-usage): How credits are calculated
266: Source: https://docs.reducto.ai/agent-guide/index.mdx

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.devin.ai/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Authentication
5: > Understand principals, tokens, and how to authenticate with the Devin API
6: The Devin API uses a **principal + token** model. A **principal** is who you are (your identity), and a **token** is how you prove it (your credential). Understanding this distinction is the key to choosing the right authentication method for your use case.
7: ## Principals & tokens
8: | Principal | Token | Description |
9: | - | - | - |
10: | **Service User** (non-human) | Service User API Key | For automated integrations and CI/CD pipelines |
11: | **User** (human) | Personal Access Token (PAT) | For human programmatic access under your own identity |
12: All API credentials use the `cog_` prefix format. Include your token in the `Authorization` header of every request:
13: ```bash theme={null}
14: curl -X GET "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
15: -H "Authorization: Bearer cog_your_token_here"
16: ```
17: The key distinction is **which principal the token authenticates as**:
18: * A **Service User API Key** authenticates as the **service user** — the service user's identity, permissions, and org memberships apply.
19: * A **Personal Access Token** authenticates as the **human user** who created it — that user's identity, permissions, and org memberships apply.
20: ### Personal access token or service user?
21: | | Personal access token | Service user API key |
22: | - | - | - |
23: | **Acts as** | You | A separate non-human identity |
24: | **Permissions** | Exactly yours, in every organization you have access to | The role you give the service user, in the organizations it is added to |
25: | **Scope** | Your account. Each request names the organization | Created at the organization or enterprise level |
26: | **Audit trail** | Attributed to you | Attributed to the service user, even when it creates a session on someone's behalf with `create_as_user_id` |
27: | **Lifecycle** | Tied to you. Revoked automatically if you leave the account | Not tied to any person, so it survives team changes |
28: | **Best for** | Personal scripts, local tooling, the Devin CLI and desktop apps | CI/CD, production integrations, shared automation |
29: Rule of thumb: if the integration should keep working after you leave the team or change roles, use a service user. If it should do exactly what you can do, as you, use a PAT.
30: ***
31: ## Service users (recommended for automation)
32: Service users are non-human accounts designed for API integrations. They can be assigned specific permissions via RBAC and added to organizations independently of human users.
33: ### How it works
34: 1. **Provision a service user** in **Settings > Devin API** (**Service users** tab) for an organization, or **Enterprise settings > Devin API** (**Service users** tab) for the enterprise
35: 2. **Assign a role** that controls which endpoints the service user can access. You pick a role from a dropdown, not individual permissions
36: 3. **Choose an expiration** — it defaults to 30 days; the other options are 7 days, 90 days, and, where your account allows it, Never
37: 4. **Copy the API key** — the key starts with `cog_` and is shown only once, right after provisioning
38: 5. **Use the key** in the `Authorization` header of every API request
39: ```bash theme={null}
40: curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
41: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY" \
42: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
43: -d '{"prompt": "Create a simple Python script"}'
44: ```
45: ### Service user scopes
46: | Scope | Created in | API access | Use case |
47: | - | - | - | - |
48: | **Organization** | Settings > Devin API > Service users | `/v3/organizations/*` | Session management, knowledge, playbooks, secrets |
49: | **Enterprise** | Enterprise settings > Devin API > Service users | `/v3/enterprise/*` + `/v3/organizations/*` | Cross-org management, analytics, audit logs, billing |
50: > [!TIP]
51: >
52: > Find your organization ID at the top of the **Settings > Devin API** page.
53: ### Session attribution with `create_as_user_id`
54: Service users are separate identities from human users. By default, sessions created by a service user are attributed to the service user itself. To create sessions **on behalf of a specific user**, pass the `create_as_user_id` parameter when creating a session. The session will appear in that user's session list and count toward their usage.
55: This requires the `ImpersonateOrgSessions` permission on the service user's role.
56: ### Key properties
57: * Keys start with `cog_` and are shown only once at creation time
58: * Service users appear separately from human users in audit logs
59: * Permissions are controlled via RBAC — assign only what the integration needs
60: * Enterprise service users inherit org-level permissions across all organizations
61: For detailed setup instructions, see the [Teams quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/teams-quickstart.md) or [Enterprise quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/enterprise-quickstart.md).
62: ***
63: ## Personal access tokens
64: Personal Access Tokens (PATs) allow human users to authenticate programmatically under their own identity. When you use a PAT, the API sees **you** — your permissions, your org memberships, and your audit trail.
65: This is useful when you want to make API calls as yourself (e.g., personal scripts, local tooling) rather than through a shared service user.
66: A PAT is not scoped to an organization or an enterprise. It belongs to you within your account and works in every organization you have access to. Each request names an organization in the URL, and your role in that organization decides what the request can do.
67: For enterprise accounts, PATs are governed by an enterprise-wide policy (disabled by default) that enterprise admins configure — including an approval workflow and mandatory token expiration.
68: For more details, see [Personal Access Tokens](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/personal-access-tokens.md).
69: ***
70: ## Legacy authentication (deprecated)
71: > [!WARNING]
72: >
73: > Legacy API keys are deprecated. Use [API v3](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/overview.md) with service user authentication. See the [migration guide](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/migration-guide.md).
74: Legacy API keys are used with the v1 and v2 APIs. They continue to work during the deprecation period but do not support new features like RBAC, session attribution, or cursor-based pagination.
75: | Key type | Prefix | Used with | Description |
76: | - | - | - | - |
77: | **Personal API key** | `apk_user_` | v1, v2 | Tied to a user account, inherits user permissions |
78: | **Service API key** | `apk_` | v1 | Organization-scoped, for automation |
79: **Where to generate:** [Settings > API Keys](https://app.devin.ai/settings/api-keys)
80: ***
81: ## Security best practices
82: > [!WARNING]
83: >
84: > Never share API keys in publicly accessible areas such as GitHub repositories, client-side code, or logs.
85: 1. **Store keys securely**: Use environment variables or secret management systems
86: 2. **Rotate keys regularly**: Generate new keys and revoke old ones periodically
87: 3. **Use service users for automation**: Prefer service users over personal keys for production
88: 4. **Apply least privilege**: Grant only the minimum permissions required
89: 5. **Monitor usage**: Review audit logs for unexpected API activity
90: 6. **Revoke compromised keys immediately**: If a key is exposed, revoke it and generate a new one. In **Settings > Devin API**, a service user's key has no revoke or rotate button: use **Delete service user** on its row, which stops the key immediately, then provision a new one. Enterprises can also [revoke](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/service-users/delete-enterprise-service-user-api-key.md) or [rotate](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/service-users/rotate-enterprise-service-user-api-key.md) a service user's key through the API (beta)
91: ## Troubleshooting
92: ### 401 Unauthorized
93: **Possible causes:**
94: * Invalid or expired API key
95: * Missing `Authorization` header
96: * Incorrect Bearer token format
97: * Using a legacy API key (`apk_` / `apk_user_`) with the [Devin MCP](https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/devin-mcp.md) — only `cog_`-prefixed keys are supported
98: **Solution:** Verify your API key is correct and properly formatted in the Authorization header. For MCP usage, ensure you are using a service user API key (not a legacy key).
99: ### 403 Forbidden
100: **Possible causes:**
101: * API key doesn't have required permissions
102: * Using the wrong key type for the endpoint (e.g., legacy key with v3 endpoints)
103: * Attempting to access resources outside your scope
104: **Solution:**
105: * Ensure your service user has the correct role and permissions
106: * For legacy v2 endpoints: ensure you have the Enterprise Admin role
107: * For legacy v1 endpoints: verify you have access to the organization
108: ### 404 Not Found
109: **Possible causes:**
110: * Incorrect API endpoint URL
111: * Resource doesn't exist or you don't have access
112: **Solution:** Verify the endpoint URL and that the resource exists.
113: ## Next steps
114: * [Teams quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/teams-quickstart.md) — get started in minutes
115: * [Enterprise quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/enterprise-quickstart.md) — RBAC and multi-org setup
116: * [Common flows](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/common-flows.md) — end-to-end workflow examples
117: * [Migration guide](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/migration-guide.md) — migrate from v1/v2
118: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.devin.ai/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Devin MCP
5: > Set up the official Devin MCP server so external AI tools can manage sessions, playbooks, knowledge, and repository docs.
6: The Devin MCP server provides programmatic access to Devin's platform capabilities for both private and public repositories. Beyond repository documentation and search, it gives any MCP-compatible AI agent or IDE full access to session management, playbooks, knowledge, and scheduling.
7: > [!NOTE]
8: >
9: > Any Devin session or MCP-compatible client can create sessions, manage playbooks and knowledge, set up schedules, and more. See [Advanced Capabilities](https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/advanced-capabilities.md) for details on what Devin can do.
10: ## What is MCP?
11: The [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction) (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI apps to securely connect to MCP-compatible data sources and tools. You can think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications — a standardized way to connect AI apps to different services.
12: ## Devin MCP Server
13: The Devin MCP server is an authenticated service that provides access to both public and private repositories, plus full platform management capabilities.
14: **Base Server URL:** `https://mcp.devin.ai/`
15: ### Authentication Required
16: To use the Devin MCP server, you need a Devin API key:
17: 1. Sign up for a Devin account at [Devin.ai](https://devin.ai/)
18: 2. Generate an API key from your [account settings](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/authentication.md)
19: 3. Include the API key in your MCP client configuration
20: The MCP server supports the same authentication methods as the [Devin API](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/authentication.md):
21: | Token type | Prefix | Org resolution |
22: | - | - | - |
23: | **Org-scoped service user key** | `cog_` | Automatic — org\_id is resolved from the service user |
24: | **Enterprise service user key** | `cog_` | Requires `X-Org-Id` header (see below) |
25: | **Personal access token** | `cog_` | Requires `X-Org-Id` header (see below) |
26: > [!NOTE]
27: >
28: > Legacy API keys (`apk_` / `apk_user_` prefix) only work with the repository documentation tools (`read_wiki_structure`, `read_wiki_contents`, `ask_wiki_question`, `list_wiki_repos`). The session, playbook, knowledge, schedule, and integration tools reject them because they cannot be resolved to an organization. Use a [service user API key](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/authentication.md#service-users-recommended-for-automation) for those.
29: #### Enterprise accounts: `X-Org-Id` header
30: Enterprise service user keys and PATs are scoped to the account level, not a specific organization. Since the MCP tools operate on organization-level resources (sessions, playbooks, knowledge, etc.), you must tell the server which organization to target by passing the `X-Org-Id` header:
31: ```json theme={null}
32: {
33: "mcpServers": {
34: "devin": {
35: "serverUrl": "https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp",
36: "headers": {
37: "Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>",
38: "X-Org-Id": "<YOUR_ORG_ID>"
39: }
40: }
41: }
42: }
43: ```
44: > [!TIP]
45: >
46: > Find your organization ID at the top of the **Settings > Devin API** page.
47: Org-scoped service user keys do not need this header — the organization is resolved automatically.
48: ## Available Tools
49: ### Repository Documentation
50: These tools let you explore and query documentation for any GitHub repository (public or private with authentication):
51: | Tool | Description |
52: | - | - |
53: | **`read_wiki_structure`** | Get a list of documentation topics for a GitHub repository |
54: | **`read_wiki_contents`** | View full documentation about a GitHub repository |
55: | **`ask_wiki_question`** | Ask any question about one or more repositories (up to 10) and get an answer grounded in their DeepWiki |
56: | **`list_wiki_repos`** | List the repositories that have a DeepWiki index and can be queried with your Devin account |
57: | **`generate_wiki`** | Generate (or regenerate) the DeepWiki for a connected repository and wait for it to complete |
58: > [!NOTE]
59: >
60: > `ask_wiki_question` and `list_wiki_repos` were previously named `ask_question` and `list_available_repos`. The old names are still accepted for existing integrations but are no longer advertised in the server's tool list.
61: ### Session Management
62: Create, search, inspect, and control Devin sessions programmatically:
63: | Tool | Description |
64: | - | - |
65: | **`devin_session_create`** | Create one or more Devin sessions. Each session can have a prompt, title, playbook, tags, and ACU limit |
66: | **`devin_session_search`** | Search and filter sessions by tags, playbook, origin, schedule, user, or creation/update time |
67: | **`devin_session_interact`** | Interact with a session — get status, send messages, sleep, terminate, archive, read messages and attachments, or manage tags |
68: | **`devin_session_events`** | Inspect events within a session — list summaries, fetch full event details, or search event contents by text |
69: | **`devin_session_gather`** | Wait for multiple sessions to reach a settled state (finished, errored, sleeping, or waiting) before returning. Useful after creating parallel sessions instead of polling in a loop |
70: ### Playbook Management
71: Create and manage playbooks that standardize how Devin performs tasks:
72: | Tool | Description |
73: | - | - |
74: | **`devin_playbook_manage`** | List, get, create, update, or delete playbooks. Supports automation macros (e.g. `!my_macro`) |
75: ### Knowledge Management
76: Maintain your organization's knowledge base that Devin uses for context:
77: | Tool | Description |
78: | - | - |
79: | **`devin_knowledge_manage`** | Full CRUD for knowledge notes — list, get, create, update, delete, browse folder structure. Also manage knowledge suggestions — list, view, and dismiss pending suggestions. Supports filtering by repo, folder, and search queries |
80: ### Schedule Management
81: Set up recurring or one-time scheduled Devin sessions:
82: | Tool | Description |
83: | - | - |
84: | **`devin_schedule_manage`** | List, get, create, update, or delete schedules. Supports cron expressions for recurring schedules, one-time scheduling, notification preferences, and agent selection |
85: ### Integration Management
86: View and manage your organization's native integrations and MCP servers:
87: | Tool | Description |
88: | - | - |
89: | **`devin_list_integrations`** | List all native integrations (e.g. GitHub, Jira, Slack) and MCP servers with their install status and settings URLs. Filter by installed, not installed, or all (the legacy name `list_integrations` is still accepted) |
90: | **`devin_mcp_server_manage`** | Install (from the marketplace or a custom configuration), update, enable, disable, or delete your organization's MCP servers |
91: ### Automations, Reviews, and Code Scans
92: Operate other Devin products from the same server:
93: | Tool | Description |
94: | - | - |
95: | **`devin_automation_manage`** | List, get, create, update, delete, validate, or run [automations](https://docs.devin.ai/product-guides/automations.md). Call it with `action="schemas"` first to get the supported trigger and action shapes |
96: | **`devin_review_manage`** | Trigger a [Devin Review](https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/devin-review.md) for a pull request, poll its status, and fetch a completed review's findings |
97: | **`devin_code_scan_manage`** | Manage [code scans](https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/code-scans.md): list and create scan profiles, start scans, and list or remediate findings. Requires code scanning to be enabled for the organization |
98: ### Organization Utilities
99: | Tool | Description |
100: | - | - |
101: | **`devin_user_list`** | List the organization's users (ID, email, name, and optionally roles) |
102: | **`devin_find_setting`** | Find a Devin webapp setting and get a deep-link URL to it |
103: ## Wire Protocols
104: The Devin MCP server supports Streamable HTTP:
105: * **URL:** `https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp`
106: * Works with HTTP-compatible clients
107: * **Recommended for all integrations**
108: > [!NOTE]
109: >
110: > The legacy SSE (`/sse`) endpoint has been deprecated. Use the `/mcp` endpoint instead.
111: ## Key Differences from DeepWiki MCP
112: | Feature | DeepWiki MCP | Devin MCP |
113: | - | - | - |
114: | **Authentication** | None required | API key required |
115: | **Repository Access** | Public repositories only | Public and private repositories |
116: | **Platform Management** | Not available | Sessions, playbooks, knowledge, schedules, integrations, automations, reviews, code scans |
117: | **Base URL** | `https://mcp.deepwiki.com/` | `https://mcp.devin.ai/` |
118: | **Cost** | Free | Requires Devin account |
119: ## Setup Instructions
120: The field name for the server URL depends on the client: Devin Desktop accepts either `serverUrl` or `url`, while most other clients only accept the standard `url` field. Using a field name your client does not recognize causes the MCP server to be silently ignored.
121: Use a personal access token or a service user key as `<API_KEY>`. `X-Org-Id` selects the organization the tools act in; find your organization ID at the top of the **Settings > Devin API** page. You can leave the header out with an org-scoped service user key.
122: ### For Devin Desktop:
123: ```json theme={null}
124: {
125: "mcpServers": {
126: "devin": {
127: "serverUrl": "https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp",
128: "headers": {
129: "Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>",
130: "X-Org-Id": "<YOUR_ORG_ID>"
131: }
132: }
133: }
134: }
135: ```
136: ### For most other clients (e.g. Cursor):
137: ```json theme={null}
138: {
139: "mcpServers": {
140: "devin": {
141: "url": "https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp",
142: "headers": {
143: "Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>",
144: "X-Org-Id": "<YOUR_ORG_ID>"
145: }
146: }
147: }
148: }
149: ```
150: ### For Claude Code:
151: ```bash theme={null}
152: claude mcp add -s user -t http devin https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp -H "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" -H "X-Org-Id: <YOUR_ORG_ID>"
153: ```

159: * **[DeepWiki MCP](https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/deepwiki-mcp.md)** — For public repositories only
160: * **[DeepWiki](https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/deepwiki.md)**

120: ### Automation

317: - [Create knowledge entry](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/knowledge/create-knowledge.md): Create a new knowledge entry for the organization.
318: - [Update knowledge entry](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/knowledge/update-knowledge.md): Update an existing knowledge entry.
319: - [Delete knowledge entry](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/knowledge/delete-knowledge.md): Delete a knowledge entry from the organization.
320: #### Playbooks Endpoints
321: - [List Playbooks](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/playbooks/list-playbooks.md): Retrieve all playbooks accessible to your organization
322: - [Create Playbook](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/playbooks/create-playbook.md): Create a new team playbook
323: - [Get Playbook](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/playbooks/get-playbook.md): Retrieve details of a specific playbook
324: - [Update Playbook](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/playbooks/update-playbook.md): Update an existing team playbook
325: - [Delete Playbook](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/playbooks/delete-playbook.md): Delete a team playbook
326: #### Secrets Endpoints
327: - [List secrets](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/secrets/list-secrets.md): List metadata for all organization secrets with the Devin v1 API. Returns IDs, types, names, and creation times, never secret values.
328: - [Create Secret](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/secrets/create-secret.md): Create a new encrypted organization secret with the Devin v1 API. Supports cookie, key-value, and TOTP types.
329: - [Delete a secret](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v1/secrets/delete-secret.md): Permanently delete an organization secret by its ID with the Devin v1 API. This action cannot be undone.
330: ### Legacy API v2
331: - [v2 API Overview (Legacy)](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/overview.md): Enterprise-wide management, analytics, and compliance for administrators
332: #### API Key Endpoints
333: - [Create a Service API Key](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/api-keys/provision-service-key.md): Provision a service API key for an Organization in the Enterprise
334: - [List API Keys](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/api-keys/list-enterprise-api-keys.md): List API keys across an Enterprise
335: - [Revoke API Key](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/api-keys/revoke-enterprise-api-key.md): Revoke a specific enterprise API key
336: #### Audit Log Endpoints
337: - [Get Audit Logs](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/audit-logs.md): Retrieve audit logs for the entire enterprise.
338: #### Consumption Endpoints
339: - [Consumption Cycles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/consumption-cycles.md): Generate a list of all billing cycles for the enterprise
340: - [Daily Consumption](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/daily-consumption.md): Get daily ACU consumption for your enterprise by date and organization for a date range, defaulting to the current billing cycle.
341: - [User Daily Consumption](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/user-daily-consumption.md): Return daily ACU consumption for one enterprise user by date and organization. The default range is the current billing cycle.
342: #### Groups Endpoints
343: - [List Enterprise Groups](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/groups/list-enterprise-groups.md): List IdP groups in this Enterprise
344: - [Get Group Details](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/groups/get-group-details.md): Get details for a specific IdP group in this Enterprise
345: #### Infrastructure Endpoints
346: - [List Hypervisors](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/infrastructure/list-enterprise-hypervisors.md): Get hypervisor status information for VPC monitoring
347: #### Members Endpoints
348: - [List Enterprise Members](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/members/list-enterprise-members.md): List paginated members in this enterprise
349: - [Get Member Details](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/members/get-member-details.md): Get detailed information about a specific enterprise member
350: - [Delete Enterprise Member](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/members/delete-enterprise-member.md): Remove a user from an organization
351: - [User Organizations](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/members/user-organizations.md): Get paginated list of organizations that this user has access to
352: - [Invite Enterprise Members](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/members/invite-enterprise-members.md): Invite multiple users to the enterprise by email (bulk invite, max 100 users)
353: #### Metrics Endpoints
354: - [PR Metrics](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/pr-metrics.md): Get pull request metrics for your enterprise
355: - [Sessions Metrics](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/sessions-metrics.md): Get sessions metrics for your enterprise
356: - [Searches Metrics](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/searches-metrics.md): Get the count of Ask Devin searches across your enterprise for a time period, excluding searches that Devin Review creates while reviewing PRs.
357: - [Usage Metrics](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/consumption/usage-metrics.md): Get usage metrics (sessions, searches, and PRs) for your enterprise
358: #### Organizations Endpoints
359: ##### Organizations
360: - [List Organizations](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/list-organizations.md): List paginated organizations in this enterprise
361: - [Create Organization](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/create-organization.md): Create a new organization in this enterprise
362: - [Get Organization Details](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/get-organization-details.md): Get details for a specific organization in this enterprise
363: - [Update Organization](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/update-organization.md): Update an organization's ACU limit and/or display name
364: - [Delete Organization](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/delete-organization.md): Delete an organization from this enterprise
365: ##### Organization Groups
366: - [Organization Groups](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/organization-groups.md): Get paginated list of enterprise groups that are in this organization
367: - [Add Group to Organization](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/add-group-to-organization.md): Add a new IdP group to an organization
368: ##### Organization Members
369: - [Organization Members](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/organization-members.md): Get paginated list of users that are in this organization
370: - [Add Organization Members](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/add-organization-members.md): Bulk add users to one or more organizations within your enterprise
371: - [Remove User from Organization](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/remove-user-from-organization.md): Remove a user from an organization
372: - [Update organization member roles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/update-organization-member-roles.md): Update organization roles for specific members
373: ##### Organization Connections
374: - [Organization Connections](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/organization-connections.md): Get paginated list of git connections that this organization has access to
375: ##### Organization Permissions
376: - [Organization Permissions](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/organization-permissions.md): Get paginated list of git permissions that this organization has access to
377: - [Add Organization Permissions](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/add-organization-permissions.md): Add git permissions to an organization
378: - [Delete Organization Permission](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/organizations/delete-organization-permission.md): Remove a git permission from an organization
379: #### Playbooks Endpoints
380: - [List Enterprise Playbooks](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/playbooks/list-playbooks.md): List all enterprise playbooks available to the authenticated user
381: - [Create Enterprise Playbook](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/playbooks/create-playbook.md): Create a new playbook in your enterprise
382: #### Repository Endpoints (Beta)
383: - [Get Repository Indexing Status](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/repositories/get-repository-status.md): Retrieve the indexing status of repositories for a specific organization.
384: - [Bulk Index Repositories](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/repositories/bulk-index-repositories.md): Index multiple repositories (up to 100) for use in Devin sessions.
385: #### Roles Endpoints
386: - [List available roles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/members/list-roles.md): List all roles that are available to the user's enterprise
387: #### Sessions Endpoints
388: ##### Enterprise Sessions
389: - [List Enterprise Sessions](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/sessions/list-enterprise-sessions.md): Get a paginated list of Devin sessions for your enterprise
390: - [List Enterprise Sessions (Insights)](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/sessions/list-enterprise-sessions-insights.md): Get a paginated list of Devin sessions with detailed analysis data for your enterprise
391: - [Get Enterprise Session](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/sessions/get-enterprise-session.md): Get detailed information about a specific Devin session including analysis data and pull requests
392: ##### Organization Sessions
393: - [List Organization Sessions](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/sessions/list-organization-sessions.md): Get a paginated list of Devin sessions for a specific organization
394: - [List Organization Sessions (Insights)](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/sessions/list-organization-sessions-insights.md): Get a paginated list of Devin sessions with detailed analysis data for a specific organization
395: #### Self Endpoints
396: - [Get Self](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/self/get-self.md): Get information about the authenticated API key
397: #### User Usage Endpoints (Beta)
398: - [Get User Usage Analysis (Beta)](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v2/user-usage/get-user-usage-analysis-beta.md): Get paginated user usage analysis with detailed ACU consumption metrics across different time periods

137: Add and manage data sources in a notebook (API)
138: Stay organized with collections
139: Save and categorize content based on your preferences.
140: Preview
141: This feature is
142: subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the
143: Service Specific
144: Terms.
145: Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support.
146: For more information, see the
147: launch stage descriptions.
148: After you have created your notebook, you can add various content types to it as
149: data sources. You can do so in batches or as single files. Some of the sources
150: include Google Docs, Google Slides, raw text, web content, and YouTube
151: videos.
152: This page describes how to perform the following tasks:
153: Add data sources in a batch
154: Upload a file as a source
155: Retrieve a source
156: Delete data sources from a notebook
157: Before you begin
158: If you plan to add Google Docs or Google Slides as your data source,
159: you must authorize access to Google Drive using Google user credentials. To
160: do so, run the following
161: gcloud auth login
162: command and follow the instructions in the CLI.
163: gcloud auth login --enable-gdrive-access
164: Use the US multi-regional endpoint
165: If your Gemini Notebook Enterprise subscription is in the US
166: multi-region, you can send the requests on this page to the US multi-regional
167: endpoint, discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com. A multi-regional endpoint
168: processes your requests and terminates TLS within the multi-region, so your
169: request data stays in the US while it's in transit. Using this endpoint doesn't
170: change where your notebooks are stored. For more information, see
171: Regional and multi-regional API endpoints
172: overview in the Google Cloud
173: security guide.
174: To use the US multi-regional endpoint, make the following changes to each
175: request URL on this page:
176: Replace the
177: ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com
178: host with discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com.
179: Set LOCATION to us.
180: The rest of each request stays the same. To learn how you choose your
181: subscription's multi-region, see
182: Get a subscription.
183: For the list of regional and multi-regional service endpoints, see
184: Regional and multi-regional service endpoints
185: in the Virtual Private Cloud guide.
186: Add data sources in a batch
187: To add sources to a notebook, call the
188: notebooks.sources.batchCreate
189: method.
190: REST
191: curl -X POST \
192: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
193: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
194: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources:batchCreate" \
195: -d '{
196: "userContents": [
197: {
198: USER_CONTENT
199: }
200: ]
201: }'
202: Replace the following:
203: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
204: values:
205: us for the US multi-region
206: eu for the EU multi-region
207: global for the Global location
208: For more information, see
209: Specify a multi-region
210: for your data store.
211: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
212: LOCATION:
213: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
214: For more information, see Locations.
215: NOTEBOOK_ID: The unique identifier of the notebook.
216: USER_CONTENT: The data source content.
217: You can add only one of the following data sources as your content:
218: For Google Drive content consisting of Google Docs or Google Slides,
219: add:
220: "googleDriveContent": {
221: "documentId": "DOCUMENT_ID_GOOGLE",
222: "mimeType": "MIME_TYPE",
223: "sourceName": "DISPLAY_NAME_GOOGLE"
224: }
225: Replace the following:
226: DOCUMENT_ID_GOOGLE: the ID of the file that's
227: in the Google Drive. This ID appears in the URL of the file. To get the
228: document ID of a file, open the file. Its URL has the pattern:
229: https://docs.google.com/FILE_TYPE/d/DOCUMENT_ID_GOOGLE/edit?resourcekey=RESOURCE_KEY.
230: MIME_TYPE: the mime type of the selected
231: document. Use application/vnd.google-apps.document for
232: Google Docs or application/vnd.google-apps.presentation
233: for Google Slides.
234: DISPLAY_NAME_GOOGLE: the display name of the
235: data source.
236: For raw text input, add:
237: "textContent": {
238: "sourceName": "DISPLAY_NAME_TEXT",
239: "content": "TEXT_CONTENT"
240: }
241: Replace the following:
242: DISPLAY_NAME_TEXT: the display name of the
243: data source.
244: TEXT_CONTENT: the raw text content that you want
245: to upload as a data source.
246: For web content, add:
247: "webContent": {
248: "url": "URL_WEBCONTENT",
249: "sourceName": "DISPLAY_NAME_WEB"
250: }
251: Replace the following:
252: URL_WEBCONTENT: the URL of the content that you
253: want to upload as a data source.
254: DISPLAY_NAME_WEB: the display name of the
255: data source.
256: For video content, add:
257: "videoContent": {
258: "youtubeUrl": "URL_YOUTUBE"
259: }
260: Replace URL_YOUTUBE with the URL of the YouTube
261: video that you want to upload as a data source.
262: If the request is successful, you should get an instance of the
263: source
264: object as a response, similar to the following JSON. Note the
265: SOURCE_ID and
266: SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME, which are required to perform
267: other tasks, such as retrieving or deleting the data source.
268: {
269: "sources": [
270: {
271: "sourceId": {
272: "id": "SOURCE_ID"
273: },
274: "title": "DISPLAY_NAME",
275: "metadata": {
276: "xyz": "abc"
277: },
278: "settings": {
279: "status": "SOURCE_STATUS_COMPLETE"
280: },
281: "name": "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME"
282: }
283: ]
284: }
285: Upload a file as a source
286: In addition to adding data sources in batches, you can upload single files
287: that can be used as data sources in your notebook.
288: To upload a single file, call the
289: notebooks.sources.uploadFile method.
290: REST
291: curl -X POST --data-binary "@PATH/TO/FILE" \
292: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
293: -H "X-Goog-Upload-File-Name: FILE_DISPLAY_NAME" \
294: -H "X-Goog-Upload-Protocol: raw" \
295: -H "Content-Type: CONTENT_TYPE" \
296: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/upload/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources:uploadFile" \
297: Replace the following:
298: PATH/TO/FILE: the path to the file that you want
299: to upload.
300: FILE_DISPLAY_NAME: a string that denotes the
301: display name of the file in the notebook.
302: CONTENT_TYPE: the type of content that you want to
303: upload. For a list of supported content types, see
304: Supported content types.
305: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
306: values:
307: us for the US multi-region
308: eu for the EU multi-region
309: global for the Global location
310: For more information, see
311: Specify a multi-region
312: for your data store.
313: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
314: LOCATION:
315: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
316: For more information, see Locations.
317: NOTEBOOK_ID: the unique identifier of the notebook.
318: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the
319: following.
320: {
321: "sourceId": {
322: "id": "SOURCE_ID"
323: }
324: }
325: Supported content types
326: The file that you upload as a source must be supported.
327: The following document content types are supported:
328: File extension
329: Content type
330: .pdf
331: application/pdf
332: .txt
333: text/plain
334: .md
335: text/markdown
336: .docx
337: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document
338: .pptx
339: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation
340: .xlsx
341: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet
342: The following audio content types are supported:
343: File extension
344: Content type
345: .3g2
346: audio/3gpp2
347: .3gp
348: audio/3gpp
349: .aac
350: audio/aac
351: .aif
352: audio/aiff
353: .aifc
354: audio/aiff
355: .aiff
356: audio/aiff
357: .amr
358: audio/amr
359: .au
360: audio/basic
361: .avi
362: video/x-msvideo
363: .cda
364: application/x-cdf
365: .m4a
366: audio/m4a
367: .mid
368: audio/midi
369: .midi
370: audio/midi
371: .mp3
372: audio/mpeg
373: .mp4
374: video/mp4
375: .mpeg
376: audio/mpeg
377: .ogg
378: audio/ogg
379: .opus
380: audio/ogg
381: .ra
382: audio/vnd.rn-realaudio
383: .ram
384: audio/vnd.rn-realaudio
385: .snd
386: audio/basic
387: .wav
388: audio/wav
389: .weba
390: audio/webm
391: .wma
392: audio/x-ms-wma
393: The following image content types are supported:
394: File extension
395: Content type
396: .png
397: image/png
398: .jpg
399: image/jpg
400: .jpeg
401: image/jpeg
402: Retrieve a source
403: To retrieve a specific source that's added to a notebook, use the
404: notebooks.sources.get
405: method.
406: REST
407: curl -X GET \
408: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
409: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
410: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources/SOURCE_ID"
411: Replace the following:
412: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
413: values:
414: us for the US multi-region
415: eu for the EU multi-region
416: global for the Global location
417: For more information, see
418: Specify a multi-region
419: for your data store.
420: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
421: LOCATION:
422: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
423: For more information, see Locations.
424: NOTEBOOK_ID: the unique identifier
425: that you received when you created the notebook. For more information, see
426: Create a notebook.
427: SOURCE_ID: the source's identifier
428: that you received when you added the source to your notebook.
429: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the following.
430: {
431: "sources": [
432: {
433: "sourceId": {
434: "id": "SOURCE_ID"
435: },
436: "title": "DISPLAY_NAME",
437: "metadata": {
438: "wordCount": 148,
439: "tokenCount": 160
440: },
441: "settings": {
442: "status": "SOURCE_STATUS_COMPLETE"
443: },
444: "name": "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME"
445: }
446: ]
447: }
448: Delete data sources from a notebook
449: To delete data sources in bulk from a notebook, use the
450: notebooks.sources.batchDelete
451: method.
452: REST
453: curl -X POST \
454: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
455: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
456: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources:batchDelete" \
457: -d '{
458: "names": [
459: "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME_1",
460: "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME_2"
461: ]
462: }'
463: Replace the following:
464: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
465: values:
466: us for the US multi-region
467: eu for the EU multi-region
468: global for the Global location
469: For more information, see

472: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
473: LOCATION:
474: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
475: For more information, see Locations.
476: NOTEBOOK_ID: The unique identifier of the notebook.
477: SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME: the complete resource name
478: of the data source to be deleted. This field has the pattern:
479: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/source/SOURCE_ID.
480: If the request is successful, you should receive an empty JSON object.

140: This page describes how to get subscriptions for Gemini Notebook Enterprise,
141: assign licenses to your users, and what to do when subscriptions expire.
142: Note: NotebookLM Enterprise is renamed to
143: Gemini Notebook Enterprise, but the subscription name remains
144: NotebookLM Enterprise.
145: About licenses
146: To sign in to the Gemini Notebook Enterprise app, a user must have
147: a license. Licenses can be assigned to users manually or automatically.
148: Manually-assigned licenses: These belong to an individual user and are
149: associated with the user's email address.
150: Manually-assigned licenses are best for users who rely on the
151: Gemini Notebook Enterprise app and use it often.
152: Automatically-assigned licenses: You can choose to have licenses that are
153: part of a subscription be automatically assigned to a user the first time
154: that the user accesses the Gemini Notebook Enterprise interface.
155: This is a way to distribute licenses in bulk without having to assign licenses
156: to each individual separately.
157: Licenses are specific to multi-region. For example, if users want access to
158: notebooks in both the us multi-region and global, assign them a license in
159: each.
160: About subscriptions
161: You buy licenses by the subscription. A subscription contains at least 15
162: licenses and can contain up to 5,000 licenses. If you need more than 5,000
163: licenses, contact your Google sales representative.
164: Subscriptions are specific to multi-regions. Users who create notebooks
165: in the global region need licenses from a global subscription. Similarly,
166: users who need to keep their notebooks and data in the European Union need
167: licenses from an eu subscription.
168: There are two subscription tiers for Gemini Notebook Enterprise:
169: The free-trial tier: With this tier, you get a full-featured, 14-day trial
170: subscription of 5000 licenses.
171: The paid tier: You can buy a monthly subscription or a year-long
172: subscription. Both the monthly and the yearly subscriptions can be set to renew
173: automatically.
174: Before you begin
175: Before starting the procedures on this page, make sure that:
176: You have completed the tasks on the
177: Set up Gemini Notebook Enterprise. This includes granting
178: at least the Cloud NotebookLM User (roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmUser)
179: role to any users who you'll license to use
180: Gemini Notebook Enterprise (including free-trial users).
181: You have the following roles:
182: Cloud NotebookLM Admin (roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmOwner)
183: Gemini Enterprise Admin (roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin)
184: Get a subscription
185: A paid subscription is billed to the Cloud Billing account that's linked to
186: your project when you add the subscription. You don't choose a billing account
187: on the Add subscription page. For more information about switching billing
188: accounts, see Switch to a different billing
189: account.
190: To get a subscription for Gemini Notebook Enterprise, do the
191: following:
192: Optional: To have the subscription billed to a different billing account,
193: link your project to that billing account. For more information, see
194: Change the Cloud Billing account linked to a
195: project.
196: This change also moves the project's other Google Cloud charges to that
197: billing account.
198: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
199: Gemini Enterprise
200: Click Manage users.
201: Choose a Multi-region for your subscription. If you don't have
202: compliance or regulatory reasons to locate your data in the US or EU
203: multi-regions, Google recommends that you choose the global region for
204: maximum availability and low latency.
205: Click add Add
206: subscription.
207: On the Add subscription page:
208: Enter the Number of licenses that you want.
209: Choose the Term for the subscription.
210: Optional: Click Auto renew.
211: Select your tier.
212: Click Add.
213: Switch to a different billing account
214: You might need to bill your Gemini Notebook Enterprise licenses
215: to a different Cloud Billing account, for example, if your
216: organization moves to a new one. The Edit subscription page doesn't let
217: you change a subscription's billing account. Instead, you create a new
218: subscription that's billed to the new billing account and transfer your users
219: to it.
220: To switch billing accounts, follow these steps:
221: If auto renew is on for the existing subscription, turn it off:
222: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
223: Gemini Enterprise
224: Click Manage users.
225: Select the Multi-region of the existing subscription.
226: Click Edit for the subscription, clear Auto renew, and then
227: click Save. If Edit isn't available for the subscription,
228: contact your Google sales representative.
229: Link your project to the new billing account. For more information, see
230: Change the Cloud Billing account linked to a
231: project.
232: This change also moves the project's other Google Cloud charges to the
233: new billing account.
234: Get a subscription in the same multi-region. The new
235: subscription is billed to the new billing account, starting as soon as you
236: add it. Your existing subscription is typically still billed to the old
237: billing account until its term ends.
238: Important: To avoid paying for overlapping subscriptions, add the new
239: subscription shortly before the existing one expires. If the existing
240: subscription expires before you add the new one, users can't sign in until
241: you transfer them to the new subscription.
242: Transfer your users to the new subscription, either
243: manually or automatically when the existing
244: subscription expires.
245: Add users and manually assign them licenses
246: To manually assign licenses to users from a subscription, do the following:
247: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
248: Gemini Enterprise
249: Click Manage users.
250: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
251: Click Add users.
252: On the Add users page:
253: Enter the email addresses of the users. Make sure to use the same email
254: address that they'll use to sign in to the
255: Gemini Notebook Enterprise app.
256: Select the subscription to assign to those users.
257: Click Submit.
258: Add users and assign them licenses automatically
259: To assign licenses to users automatically when they sign in to the
260: Gemini Notebook Enterprise app, do the following:
261: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
262: Gemini Enterprise
263: Click Manage users.
264: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
265: Make sure that you have a subscription with enough licenses for
266: the maximum number of users that you expect be signed in to
267: Gemini Notebook Enterprise at any one time.
268: Select Assign licenses automatically and then select the subscription.
269: A license from this subscription is assigned each time a user who doesn't
270: have a manually-assigned license signs in.
271: If no licenses remain in the subscription, users are shown a message
272: notifying them that they don't have access.
273: Transfer licenses from expired subscriptions
274: Users can't sign in to Gemini Notebook Enterprise if the subscription
275: has expired. There are a couple of approaches to returning sign-in access to
276: them:
277: Automatically transfer users with expired licenses to the default
278: subscription.
279: Manually transfer users to a new subscription.
280: Automatically transfer users to an active subscription
281: To automatically transfer users to an active subscription, do the following:
282: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
283: Gemini Enterprise
284: Click Manage users.
285: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
286: Make sure that you have an active subscription. If you don't have one, get
287: a subscription.
288: Select Assign licenses automatically and choose the active subscription.
289: Select Automatically update expired license.
290: When a user with an expired license next signs in, they are automatically
291: granted a license in the chosen subscription.
292: Manually transfer users to an active subscription
293: To manually transfer users to an active subscription, do the following:
294: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
295: Gemini Enterprise
296: Click Manage users.
297: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
298: Make sure that you have an active subscription. If you don't have one, get
299: a subscription.
300: Select the users and click Assign different license.
301: In the Edit Users pane, select the subscription and click Submit.
302: What's next
303: Share the sign-in link for Gemini Notebook Enterprise with your users.
304: See step 5 of Set the identity provider for
305: Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
306: If your users need instructions on how to share notebooks or revoke sharing
307: on notebooks, see Share notebooks. Sharing is one feature
308: of Gemini Notebook that is different between the personal Gemini Notebook product and
309: Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
310: If your users need guidance on how to use Gemini Notebook, see
311: the user documentation for
312: Gemini Notebook. Note that there are some
313: differences between Gemini Notebook and Gemini Notebook Enterprise. See
314: What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
315: Send feedback
316: Except as otherwise noted, the content of this page is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License, and code samples are licensed under the Apache 2.0 License. For details, see the Google Developers Site Policies. Java is a registered trademark of Oracle and/or its affiliates.

26: Connect AI models to Otter using Model Context Protocol (MCP). Connecting Otter MCP to your AI applications enables secure, scalable access to various language model understandings to power features like smarter summaries, contextual suggestions, and automated insights for all your Otter conversations and meetings.
27: Learn to connect to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Perplexity, or other platforms.
28: What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
29: MCP is an open standard that allows AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT
30: to securely access external data sources. With Otter’s MCP Server, these AI
31: assistants can:
32: ✅ Search your meeting transcripts across all time periods
33: ✅ Analyze patterns and themes across multiple meetings
34: ✅ Generate content using your actual meeting data
35: ✅ Surface insights without leaving your AI workflow
36: 🔑 Key advantage: Your meeting knowledge becomes instantly accessible to AI
37: assistants, eliminating manual copy-paste and context-switching.
38: 🔒 Security: All access is OAuth-authenticated with granular permissions.
39: Your AI assistant can only access meetings you explicitly authorize.
40: Claude setup Learn how to set up Claude
41: Check out Otter.ai in the Claude connectors directory.
42: Connect Otter MCP to Claude.
43: Go to Settings → Connectors → Browse connectors.
44: Note: If your workspace admin has already added Otter.ai, it will appear as an available connector. Click Connect and proceed directly to Step 3.
45: Go to Claude's Otter.ai page and click Connect.
46: Sign in to your Otter account. Review the info and click Authorize access to connect with Claude.
47: Otter MCP is connected to Claude.
48: Enable Otter MCP tool with chat
49: Click on the search and tools menu in the chat box. Toggle on Otter.
50: Configure your Otter MCP tool permissions
51: Claude will prompt for permissions when querying using Otter MCP tools.
52: You can manage permissions for the Otter MCP tool in the connector settings.
53: Under the settings Connectors, click Configure next to Otter or manage through the 3-dot menu.
54: Manage each of the tools' permissions. We recommend setting it to Always allow.
55: ChatGPT setup Learn how to set up ChatGPT
56: Connect Otter MCP to ChatGPT. Otter.ai is available in the ChatGPT App Store.
57: Check out Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.
58: Sign in to the ChatGPT web version. Go to Settings.
59: Note: To connect to Otter MCP, you must currently complete the connection through the web version of Otter. Connecting directly through the desktop app is not yet supported. Once the connection is established on the web, it will automatically be available in the desktop app.
60: Go to Apps and add apps. The option may vary depending on your existing account.
61: Go to Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.
62: Click Connect.
63: Carefully review the information and click Connect Otter.ai.
64: Sign in to your Otter.ai account. Carefully review the information and click Authorize access to proceed.
65: Otter.ai is now connected to your ChatGPT account.
66: Enable Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT. Now that Otter is connected, you can work from the ChatGPT web browser or the desktop app.
67: Click the + (plus icon). Click ••• More and select Otter.ai.
68: Type @ and select Otter.ai.
69: When starting a new chat, make sure Otter.ai is showing. If you do not see otter.ai, select it again through the steps above.
70: Using Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT
71: Otter uses 3 tools in ChatGPT to query your meetings:
72: fetch
73: get user info
74: search
75: If prompted, accept the tool request to proceed.
76: You can click any source to go directly to the Otter conversation.
77: If you are experiencing any issues querying your Otter conversations, we recommend specifically mentioning the Otter tool you want to use in your query.
78: Manage Otter MCP settings for ChatGPT in Apps.
79: Cursor setup Learn how to set up Cursor
80: Connect Otter MCP to Cursor. Refer to Cursor’s documentation on connecting MCP servers for more info.
81: Navigate to Cursor settings. Click Tools & MCP. Click Add Custom MCP.
82: Configure the JSON file with the following. Save changes to the file.
83: {
84: "mcpServers": {
85: "otter_meeting_mcp": {
86: "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
87: }
88: }
89: }
90: Navigate back to Tools & MCP. Click Connect.
91: Click Open.
92: Sign in to your Otter account. Click Authorize access.
93: Otter MCP is connected to Cursor.
94: Enable Cursor
95: Enable Otter MCP by ensuring it's toggled ON under Cursor Tools & MCP settings and tools enabled. Cursor will automatically use available tools.
96: If a tool is disabled, click on the grayed-out tool to re-enable.
97: Perplexity Learn how to set up Perplexity
98: Connect Otter MCP to Perplexity using custom connectors to securely access and reference your Otter conversations, meeting notes, and AI insights directly within Perplexity.
99: Note: Perplexity’s UI may change over time. Refer to Perplexity’s documentation for the latest instructions on connecting a custom connector.
100: Navigate to the Connectors settings page. The location may vary depending on whether you are using an individual or an Enterprise account.
101: Click + Custom connector.
102: Configure using the following settings and click Add.
103: Name: Otter.ai
104: Description: Meetings from Otter
105: MCP server URL: https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp
106: Icon: The Otter icon can be downloaded here.
107: Sign in to your Otter account and click Authorize access.
108: Otter MCP is connected to Perplexity.
109: Enable Perplexity
110: Make sure the connector is enabled before submitting your query. You may need to grant permissions the first time you use the provided tools.
111: Connect Otter MCP to other AI tools You may be able to connect Otter MCP to your AI tool depending on your platform
112: Otter MCP can be connected to third-party AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP) using a JSON configuration file. Setup varies by platform and is managed entirely within your AI tool’s configuration. Configuration, behavior, and support depend on the specific platform you are using. Refer to your tool's documentation to connect to an MCP server.
113: Before you begin
114: Your AI tool must support MCP
115: You should be familiar with editing JSON configuration files
116: OAuth authentication is still required to connect
117: JSON Configuration file
118: {
119: "mcpServers": {
120: "otter": {
121: "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
122: }
123: }
124: }
125: Complete setup in your AI tool
126: Add a custom MCP and configure the JSON file with the above.
127: Connect and authenticate with your Otter account.
128: Verify the Otter MCP server appears, and tools are available.
129: Note: We’ll continue adding step-by-step guides for more AI tools. In the meantime, setup may vary by platform and is completed at your discretion.
130: Tools overview
131: Name
132: Description
133: Sample prompt
134: Get user info
135: Get the current user's name and email. This tool retrieves the authenticated user's profile information, including their name and email address.
136: “What is my email address?”
137: Search
138: Search for meetings and get an overview of information.
139: "Which meetings related to product improvement did I attend in Q2?"
140: Fetch
141: Retrieves a full speech transcript of a meeting or conversation.
142: "What are the three main focus areas based on marketing meetings with our Enterprise clients?"
143: “Summarize the presentation https://otter.ai/u/NpsJNrxvrcDay0dnlPKPZM87OSo?tab=chat&view=summary”
144: Fetch example
145: Query direct conversation URLs. Copy an Otter conversation URL from the browser.
146: Note: The conversation must be shared with you for your AI application to access the content.
147: Try it out by replacing the following with your own conversation link:
148: Summarize the presentation https://otter.ai/u/NpsJNrxvrcDay0dnlPKPZM87OSo?tab=chat&view=summary
149: Examples & usage
150: Query conversations, pull highlights and key details, and generate content based on your meetings.
151: Examples
152: Generate a PowerPoint based on meeting XYZ.
153: In which meetings did we discuss mobile navigation UX?
154: Pull all meetings in Q3 discussing sales initiatives and the top ideas.
155: Advanced Use Cases
156: Competitive Intelligence Analysis
157: “Analyze all Q4 customer calls mentioning competitors. What are the top 3 feature requests we’re losing deals over?”
158: Onboarding Acceleration
159: “Pull highlights from all sales training meetings in the last month. Create a structured onboarding doc with key processes and best practices.”
160: Executive Briefings
161: “Summarize the key decisions and action items from all leadership meetings this week. Format as a Friday exec briefing.”
162: Cross-Functional Alignment
163: “Compare what Product and Sales are saying about our Q1 roadmap. Identify any misalignments or gaps in messaging.”
164: Historical Context Retrieval
165: “What did we decide about the pricing model in our August strategy meeting? Pull the exact discussion and reasoning.”
166: Meeting Prep Intelligence
167: “I have a call with Acme Corp tomorrow. Pull all previous meetings with them and summarize: current status, open issues, and key stakeholders.”
168: FAQs
169: Is Otter MCP available for all AI applications?
170: We are working to release Otter MCP for all AI applications. Contact our Otter Support Team for help setting up Otter MCP with your AI application.
171: Note: Google Gemini's support for MCP tools is not yet available, according to this thread; however, Gemini's command line interface (CLI) does support connecting to MCPs. Refer to Google's documentation for the most up-to-date information.
172: Is Google Gemini supported?
173: No.
174: According to this thread, Google Gemini does not yet support MCP tools.
175: However, Gemini's command line interface (CLI) does support connecting to MCPs.
176: Note: Refer to Google's documentation for the most up-to-date information.
177: What meetings can I access through the MCP Server?
178: You can access all meetings that you have captured in Otter, as well as any meetings shared with you from other users in your Workspace.
179: Learn more about conversation sharing and Channels in Otter.
