1: {"article":{"id":35287607569687,"url":"https://otterai.zendesk.com/api/v2/help_center/en-us/articles/35287607569687.json","html_url":"https://help.otter.ai/hc/en-us/articles/35287607569687-Otter-MCP-Server","author_id":1902597107005,"comments_disabled":true,"draft":false,"promoted":false,"position":0,"vote_sum":16,"vote_count":36,"upvote_count":26,"downvote_count":10,"section_id":15113317866263,"created_at":"2025-09-29T23:11:31Z","updated_at":"2026-11-21T22:35:08Z","name":"Otter MCP Server","title":"Otter MCP Server","source_locale":"en-us","locale":"en-us","outdated":false,"outdated_locales":[],"edited_at":"2026-10-30T21:11:48Z","user_segment_id":null,"permission_group_id":3069674,"content_tag_ids":["01H296EJXEAFDGP72EJAZJZGJJ","01K701AYA48679CA5WQG1EFKTX"],"label_names":["chatgpt","claude","cursor","otter mcp","mcp","Model Context Protocol","perplexity","add custom","custom connector","custom mcp","add a mcp"],"body":"

Connect AI models to Otter using Model Context Protocol (MCP). Connecting Otter MCP to your AI applications enables secure, scalable access to various language model understandings to power features like smarter summaries, contextual suggestions, and automated insights for all your Otter conversations and meetings.

Learn to connect to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Perplexity, or other platforms.

What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

MCP is an open standard that allows AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT
to securely access external data sources. With Otter’s MCP Server, these AI
assistants can:

✅ Search your meeting transcripts across all time periods

✅ Analyze patterns and themes across multiple meetings

✅ Generate content using your actual meeting data

✅ Surface insights without leaving your AI workflow

🔑 Key advantage: Your meeting knowledge becomes instantly accessible to AI
assistants, eliminating manual copy-paste and context-switching.

🔒 Security: All access is OAuth-authenticated with granular permissions.
Your AI assistant can only access meetings you explicitly authorize.

Claude setup Learn how to set up Claude

Check out Otter.ai in the Claude connectors directory.

Connect Otter MCP to Claude.

  1. Go to Settings → Connectors → Browse connectors.

    Note: If your workspace admin has already added Otter.ai, it will appear as an available connector. Click Connect and proceed directly to Step 3.

  2. Go to Claude's Otter.ai page and click Connect.

  3. Sign in to your Otter account. Review the info and click Authorize access to connect with Claude.

  4. Otter MCP is connected to Claude.

Enable Otter MCP tool with chat

Click on the search and tools menu in the chat box. Toggle on Otter.

Configure your Otter MCP tool permissions

Claude will prompt for permissions when querying using Otter MCP tools.

You can manage permissions for the Otter MCP tool in the connector settings.

  1. Under the settings Connectors, click Configure next to Otter or manage through the 3-dot menu.

  2. Manage each of the tools' permissions. We recommend setting it to Always allow.

ChatGPT setup Learn how to set up ChatGPT

Connect Otter MCP to ChatGPT. Otter.ai is available in the ChatGPT App Store.

Check out Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.

  1. Sign in to the ChatGPT web version. Go to Settings.

    Note: To connect to Otter MCP, you must currently complete the connection through the web version of Otter. Connecting directly through the desktop app is not yet supported. Once the connection is established on the web, it will automatically be available in the desktop app.

  2. Go to Apps and add apps. The option may vary depending on your existing account.
  3. Go to Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.
  4. Click Connect.
  5. Carefully review the information and click Connect Otter.ai.
  6. Sign in to your Otter.ai account. Carefully review the information and click Authorize access to proceed.
  7. Otter.ai is now connected to your ChatGPT account.

Enable Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT. Now that Otter is connected, you can work from the ChatGPT web browser or the desktop app.

  • Click the + (plus icon). Click ••• More and select Otter.ai.
  • Type @ and select Otter.ai.

When starting a new chat, make sure Otter.ai is showing. If you do not see otter.ai, select it again through the steps above.

Using Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT

Otter uses 3 tools in ChatGPT to query your meetings:

  • fetch
  • get user info
  • search

If prompted, accept the tool request to proceed.

You can click any source to go directly to the Otter conversation.

If you are experiencing any issues querying your Otter conversations, we recommend specifically mentioning the Otter tool you want to use in your query.

Manage Otter MCP settings for ChatGPT in Apps.

Cursor setup Learn how to set up Cursor

Connect Otter MCP to Cursor. Refer to Cursor’s documentation on connecting MCP servers for more info.

  1. Navigate to Cursor settings. Click Tools & MCP. Click Add Custom MCP.

  2. Configure the JSON file with the following. Save changes to the file.

    {
 "mcpServers": {
 "otter_meeting_mcp": {
 "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
 }
 }
}

  3. Navigate back to Tools & MCP. Click Connect.

  4. Click Open.

  5. Sign in to your Otter account. Click Authorize access.

  6. Otter MCP is connected to Cursor.

Enable Cursor

Enable Otter MCP by ensuring it's toggled ON under Cursor Tools & MCP settings and tools enabled. Cursor will automatically use available tools.

If a tool is disabled, click on the grayed-out tool to re-enable.

Perplexity Learn how to set up Perplexity

Connect Otter MCP to Perplexity using custom connectors to securely access and reference your Otter conversations, meeting notes, and AI insights directly within Perplexity.

Note: Perplexity’s UI may change over time. Refer to Perplexity’s documentation for the latest instructions on connecting a custom connector.
  1. Navigate to the Connectors settings page. The location may vary depending on whether you are using an individual or an Enterprise account.

  2. Click + Custom connector.

  3. Configure using the following settings and click Add.
    • Name: Otter.ai
    • Description: Meetings from Otter

    • MCP server URL: https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp

      Icon: The Otter icon can be downloaded here.

  4. Sign in to your Otter account and click Authorize access.

  5. Otter MCP is connected to Perplexity.

Enable Perplexity

Make sure the connector is enabled before submitting your query. You may need to grant permissions the first time you use the provided tools.

Connect Otter MCP to other AI tools You may be able to connect Otter MCP to your AI tool depending on your platform

Otter MCP can be connected to third-party AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP) using a JSON configuration file. Setup varies by platform and is managed entirely within your AI tool’s configuration. Configuration, behavior, and support depend on the specific platform you are using. Refer to your tool's documentation to connect to an MCP server.

Before you begin

  • Your AI tool must support MCP
  • You should be familiar with editing JSON configuration files
  • OAuth authentication is still required to connect

JSON Configuration file

{
 "mcpServers": {
 "otter": {
 "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
 }
 }
}

Complete setup in your AI tool

  1. Add a custom MCP and configure the JSON file with the above.
  2. Connect and authenticate with your Otter account.
  3. Verify the Otter MCP server appears, and tools are available.
Note: We’ll continue adding step-by-step guides for more AI tools. In the meantime, setup may vary by platform and is completed at your discretion.

Tools overview

Fetch example

Query direct conversation URLs. Copy an Otter conversation URL from the browser.

Note: The conversation must be shared with you for your AI application to access the content.

Try it out by replacing the following with your own conversation link:

Summarize the presentation https://otter.ai/u/NpsJNrxvrcDay0dnlPKPZM87OSo?tab=chat&view=summary

Examples & usage

Query conversations, pull highlights and key details, and generate content based on your meetings.

Examples

Generate a PowerPoint based on meeting XYZ.

In which meetings did we discuss mobile navigation UX?

Pull all meetings in Q3 discussing sales initiatives and the top ideas.

Advanced Use Cases

FAQs

Is Otter MCP available for all AI applications?

  • We are working to release Otter MCP for all AI applications. Contact our Otter Support Team for help setting up Otter MCP with your AI application.
Note: Google Gemini's support for MCP tools is not yet available, according to this thread; however, Gemini's command line interface (CLI) does support connecting to MCPs. Refer to Google's documentation for the most up-to-date information.

Is Google Gemini supported?

  • No.
  • According to this thread, Google Gemini does not yet support MCP tools.
  • However, Gemini's command line interface (CLI) does support connecting to MCPs.
Note: Refer to Google's documentation for the most up-to-date information.

What meetings can I access through the MCP Server?

  • You can access all meetings that you have captured in Otter, as well as any meetings shared with you from other users in your Workspace.
  • Learn more about conversation sharing and Channels in Otter.

Can I connect Otter MCP on the ChatGPT desktop app?

  • Connecting Otter MCP on ChatGPT desktop app is not yet available. Connect Otter MCP on the web version of ChatGPT.

Is there a public API key for me to set up Otter MCP for my AI application?

  • We currently do not have a public API key at this time. Contact our Otter Support team for help setting up Otter MCP with your AI application.

Where can I download the Otter icon?

  • You download the Otter.ai icon at the end of this article.
  • Or save the icon image below.

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.devin.ai/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Quick start: Teams
5: > Set up Devin API access for a teams or standard organization: provision a service user, copy the API key, and create your first session.
6: This guide walks you through setting up API access for **teams and standard organizations** (non-enterprise). You'll create a service user, get your credentials, and make your first API call in minutes.
7: > [!NOTE]
8: >
9: > If you're part of an enterprise with multiple organizations or custom roles, see the [Enterprise quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/enterprise-quickstart.md) instead.
10: ## Step 1: Create a service user
11: 1. Go to **Settings > Devin API** in your organization and open the **Service users** tab
12: 2. Click **Provision service user**
13: 3. Choose a descriptive display name (e.g., "CI Pipeline", "Monitoring Bot")
14: 4. Select a role in the **Organization role** dropdown. The form has no individual permission checkboxes: a service user gets its permissions from the role you pick.
15: * **Admin** — full access, including organization settings and membership
16: * **Member** — can create and manage Devin sessions and most organization resources, but not organization settings or membership
17: 5. Choose an **Expiration**. It defaults to **30 days**; the other options are 7 days, 90 days, and, where your account allows it, **Never**. After the expiration date the service user's API key stops working, so provision a replacement before then. A shorter expiration limits how long a leaked key can be used.
18: > [!TIP]
19: >
20: > Use the **Member** role for most automation. Only use **Admin** if your integration needs to manage org settings or other users.
21: ## Step 2: Copy your API key
22: 1. After you provision the service user, its API key is shown in a dialog
23: 2. Copy the key immediately — it starts with `cog_` and won't be shown again
24: 3. Store it securely as an environment variable:
25: ```bash theme={null}
26: export DEVIN_API_KEY="cog_your_key_here"
27: ```
28: ## Step 3: Make your first API call
29: Create a Devin session:
30: ```bash theme={null}
31: export DEVIN_ORG_ID="your_org_id"
32: curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
33: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY" \
34: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
35: -d '{"prompt": "Create a simple Python script that prints Hello World"}'
36: ```
37: > [!TIP]
38: >
39: > Find your organization ID at the top of the **Settings → Devin API** page.
40: > [!NOTE]
41: >
42: > **Want sessions attributed to your user?** By default, sessions are attributed to the service user. To create sessions on behalf of a specific user (so they appear in that user's session list), add `"create_as_user_id": "user_abc123"` to the request body. This requires the **Admin** role (which includes the `ImpersonateOrgSessions` permission). See [Session attribution](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/overview.md#session-attribution) for details.
43: ## Step 4: Common operations
44: ### List your sessions
45: ```bash theme={null}
46: curl "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
47: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY"
48: ```
49: ### Send a message to a running session
50: ```bash theme={null}
51: export SESSION_ID="your_session_id"
52: curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions/$SESSION_ID/messages" \
53: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY" \
54: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
55: -d '{"message": "Please also add unit tests"}'
56: ```
57: ### Manage knowledge
58: ```bash theme={null}
59: # List knowledge entries
60: curl "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/knowledge/notes" \
61: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY"
62: # Create a knowledge entry
63: curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/knowledge/notes" \
64: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY" \
65: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
66: -d '{"name": "Coding standards", "trigger": "When writing code", "body": "Use TypeScript strict mode..."}'
67: ```
68: ## Permissions for teams users
69: Teams organizations have a simple permission model:
70: | Role | Can create sessions | Can manage resources | Can manage settings |
71: | - | - | - | - |
72: | **Member** | Yes | Yes (knowledge, playbooks, secrets) | No |
73: | **Admin** | Yes | Yes | Yes |
74: > [!NOTE]
75: >
76: > Playbooks are moving to [Skills](https://docs.devin.ai/product-guides/skills.md). In a teams account that has moved, `/playbooks` writes go to the playbook's skill. An account created on or after October 24, 2026 with no playbooks gets `410` from the `/playbooks` endpoints.
77: For fine-grained role-based access control (RBAC), see the [Enterprise quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/enterprise-quickstart.md).
78: ## Next steps
79: * Browse the **Organization API** endpoints in the sidebar
80: * See [common flows](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/common-flows.md) for common integration patterns
81: * Learn about [authentication](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/authentication.md) in depth
82: * Set up [scheduled automations](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/automations/post-organizations-automations.md) for recurring tasks
83: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.devin.ai/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Permissions & RBAC
5: > Permission reference for the Devin API
6: Every API endpoint except [`GET /v3/self`](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/self/self) is gated by a specific permission. A [service user](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/authentication.md#service-users-recommended-for-automation) gets its permissions from its assigned role; a [personal access token](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/personal-access-tokens.md) has the permissions of the user who created it. The required permission for each endpoint is documented on its individual API reference page. This page provides a summary of all permissions by scope.
7: **Base URLs:**
8: * `https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/*` — endpoints scoped to a single organization
9: * `https://api.devin.ai/v3/enterprise/*` — endpoints that require enterprise-level permissions
10: > [!NOTE]
11: >
12: > **Devin Enterprise** customers with a dedicated deployment should replace `api.devin.ai` with their custom API domain (e.g., `api.your-company.devinenterprise.com`). See the [Enterprise quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/enterprise-quickstart.md) for setup details.
13: > [!TIP]
14: >
15: > Find your organization ID at the top of the **Settings → Devin API** page.
16: > [!NOTE]
17: >
18: > Some enterprise endpoints operate on specific organizations using paths like
19: > `/v3/enterprise/organizations/{org_id}/...` (for example, audit logs and tags).
20: > Even though they include an `org_id` parameter, they require **enterprise-level** permissions.
21: ## Enterprise permissions
22: | Permission | Controls |
23: | - | - |
24: | `ManageEnterpriseSettings` | Organization tags |
25: | `ViewOrganizations` | List and get organizations (read-only; also granted by `ManageOrganizations`) |
26: | `ManageOrganizations` | Create, update, and delete organizations; also grants `ViewOrganizations` |
27: | `ManageAccountMembership` | Roles, Enterprise users, Enterprise IdP groups, Enterprise service user membership, Enterprise IdP group registration |
28: | `ViewAccountMembership` | List roles, enterprise users, IdP groups, and service users (read-only; also granted by `ManageAccountMembership`) |
29: | `ManageAccountServiceUsers` | Service user provisioning (enterprise) |
30: | `UseAccountTools` | List and get knowledge notes, knowledge folders, and playbooks (enterprise, read-only; also granted by `ManageAccountKnowledge` for knowledge and `ManageAccountPlaybooks` for playbooks) |
31: | `ManageAccountKnowledge` | Create, update, and delete knowledge notes (enterprise); also grants read access |
32: | `ManageAccountPlaybooks` | Create, update, and delete playbooks (enterprise); also grants read access |
33: | `ViewGitIntegrations` | Git connections and connection repositories (read-only; also granted by `ManageGitIntegrations`) |
34: | `ManageGitIntegrations` | Create, edit, and delete Git integrations; also grants `ViewGitIntegrations` |
35: | `ViewRepoPermissions` | Git permissions (read-only; also granted by `ManageRepoPermissions`) |
36: | `ManageRepoPermissions` | Create, replace, update, and delete Git permissions |
37: | `ManageBilling` | ACU limits |
38: | `ViewAccountAuditLogs` | Audit logs (enterprise, read-only) |
39: | `ViewAccountConsumption` | Consumption cycles, Daily consumption breakdowns (Enterprise plan only) |
40: | `ViewAccountMetrics` | Usage metrics (DAU/WAU/MAU, PRs, sessions, searches, active users), Queue status |
41: | `ViewEnterpriseInfraDetails` | Hypervisors |
42: | `ManageAccountSecureModeProfiles` | [Enterprise security profiles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/security-profiles/list-enterprise-security-profiles.md) and the [enterprise default profile](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/security-profiles/patch-enterprise-security-profile-settings.md) (Beta) |
43: | `ViewAccountSessions` | Sessions list and detail (enterprise, read-only) |
44: | `ManageAccountSessions` | Send messages to sessions (enterprise) |
45: | `ViewAccountCodeScans` | [Code scans](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-list.md), [profiles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-profiles.md) and [profile details](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-profile.md), [findings](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-findings.md), and [metrics](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-metrics.md) (enterprise, read-only) |
46: | `UseAccountCodeScans` | [Start code scans](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-start.md), [start ingestion scans](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-start-ingestion.md), and [remediate findings](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/enterprise-code-scans-remediate.md) (enterprise) |
47: ## Organization permissions
48: | Permission | Controls |
49: | - | - |
50: | `ManageOrgSecrets` | Secrets CRUD |
51: | `ManageOrgSettings` | [Set the organization default platform](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/organization-settings/put-organization-default-platform.md) |
52: | `ManageSecureModeProfiles` | [Organization security profiles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/security-profiles/list-organizations-security-profiles.md) and the [organization and automations default profiles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/security-profiles/patch-organizations-security-profile-settings.md) (Beta) |
53: | `ManageOrgKnowledge` | Create, update, and delete knowledge notes (organization) |
54: | `ManageOrgPlaybooks` | Create, update, and delete playbooks (organization) |
55: | `ManageOrgServiceUsers` | Service user provisioning (organization) |
56: | `ManageOrgSchedules` | Scheduled sessions |
57: | `ViewOrgAutomations` | Automations list and detail (organization, read-only) |
58: | `ManageOrgAutomations` | Create, edit, delete automations |
59: | `UsePersonalAutomations` | Personal automations (`run_as: creator`) |
60: | `ViewOrgConsumption` | Daily consumption breakdowns (organization, Enterprise plan only) |
61: | `ViewOrgSessions` | Sessions list and detail (organization, read-only) |
62: | `ManageOrgSessions` | Send messages, terminate, archive sessions |
63: | `UseDevinSessions` | Create sessions; list and get knowledge notes, knowledge folders, and playbooks (organization, read-only) |
64: | `ImpersonateOrgSessions` | Create sessions on behalf of other users (`create_as_user_id`) |
65: | `ViewCodeScans` | [Code scans](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-list.md), [profiles](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-profiles.md) and [profile details](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-profile.md), [findings](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-findings.md), and [metrics](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-metrics.md) (organization, read-only) |
66: | `UseCodeScans` | [Start code scans](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-start.md), [start ingestion scans](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-start-ingestion.md), and [remediate findings](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/code-scans/organizations-code-scans-remediate.md) (organization) |
67: ## Permission inheritance
68: **Enterprise service users** authenticate with `/v3/enterprise/*` endpoints and can operate across all organizations. They are assigned enterprise-level roles and automatically inherit the corresponding org-level permissions in every organization (for example, `ViewAccountSessions` grants `ViewOrgSessions` in all orgs).
69: **Organization service users** are scoped to a single organization and authenticate with `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/*` endpoints only. They are assigned org-level roles.
70: ## Creating service users
71: Service users are created through the Devin UI:
72: 1. **Enterprise service users**: Enterprise settings → Devin API (**Service users** tab)
73: 2. **Organization service users**: Organization settings → Devin API (**Service users** tab)
74: For setup instructions, see the [Teams quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/teams-quickstart.md) or [Enterprise quick start](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/getting-started/enterprise-quickstart.md).

16: To authenticate API calls, the client must add the following header:
17: Copy
18: Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
19: where TOKEN is obtained by one of the methods below.
20: Token Types
21: There are three types of tokens which can have one of two access scopes.
22: Type
23: Scope
24: Personal Access Token (PAT)
25: personal
26: Generated manually from the integrations page.
27: Doesn't expire, and can be revoked at any time.
28: Workspace Access Token (WAT)
29: workspace
30: Generated manually from the integrations page.
31: Doesn't expire, and can be revoked at any time.
32: OAuth Token
33: personal,
34: workspace
35: Issued through the OAuth2 Flow.
36: Expires, must be refreshed.
37: Scope
38: personal
39: Provides the same access level as the user who authorized the token.
40: workspace
41: Provides FULL DATA ACCESS of the workspace.
42: Can be generated by workspace admins only.
43: NOTE: The workspace scope is not available on all plans.
44: Check https://grain.com/pricing to see if your plan includes Workspace API.
45: Tokens with the personal scope, including Personal Access Tokens, also authenticate the Grain MCP server at https://api.grain.com/_/mcp.
46: Tokens with the workspace scope are not accepted by the MCP server.
47: OAuth2 Flow
48: This authentication method is for developers building integrations with Grain to be used by any Grain users.
49: The API supports a standard OAuth2 Authorization Code flow, including the PKCE extension for client-side only authentication. At least one redirect URI is required to register a new client. For browser-based client applications, a list of CORS origins can also be added.
50: Authorization Code
51: Step 1
52: Obtain the client_id and client_secret (only for server-side applications) credentials.
53: Step 2
54: Open the url https://grain.com/_/public-api/oauth2/authorize with the following query params.
55: Param
56: client_id
57: Obtained separately in Step 1
58: redirect_uri
59: Must exactly match a registered redirect URI. On localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1], any port matches
60: response_type
61: Must be code
62: state
63: Optional. Grain returns it unchanged in Step 4. PKCE already protects the flow, so state is only needed if your client relies on it
64: code_challenge
65: A random string, hashed with SHA256 and base64 URL encoded
66: code_challenge_method
67: Must be S256
68: scopes
69: personal or workspace. Defaults to personal
70: Step 3
71: If the user is not already signed in to Grain, they will be prompted to sign in.
72: After being authenticated, the user will be prompted to confirm the OAuth2 connection.
73: Step 4
74: The user will be redirected to redirect_uri from Step 2 with the code query param, and state if you sent one.
75: Step 5
76: Make a POST request to generate the token.
77: See OAuth2 Generate Token
78: Diagram
79: sequenceDiagram
80: participant you as You
81: actor user as User
82: participant grain as Grain
83: Note right of you: Step 1
84: you-->>grain: Request Client ID & Secret (manually)
85: grain-->>you: Client ID & Secret
86: Note right of you: Step 2
87: user->>you: Requests OAuth
88: you->>user: Open or Redirects to oauth2/authorize
89: user->>grain: oauth2/authorize
90: Note left of grain: Step 3
91: grain->>user: Requests login
92: user->>grain: Login
93: grain->>user: Requests Confirm OAuth
94: user->>grain: Confirms
95: Note left of grain: Step 4
96: grain->>user: Redirects to redirect_uri w/code
97: user->>you: redirect_uri w/code
98: Note right of you: Step 5
99: you->>grain: POST oauth2/token w/code
100: grain->>you: access_token & refresh_token
101: Note right of you: Refresh
102: you->>grain: POST oauth2/token w/refresh_token
103: grain->>you: access_token & refresh_token
104: Client ID Metadata Document
105: Public clients, such as MCP clients and native apps, can skip Step 1 by using an HTTPS URL as their client_id.
106: That URL must serve a JSON Client ID Metadata Document describing the client.
107: Copy
108: {
109: "client_id": "https://app.example.com/oauth/client.json",
110: "client_name": "Example App",
111: "redirect_uris": ["https://app.example.com/oauth/callback"],
112: "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
113: "response_types": ["code"],
114: "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
115: }
116: Field
117: client_id
118: Required. Must exactly match the URL the document is served from
119: redirect_uris
120: Required. The redirect_uri in Step 2 must exactly match one of these
121: client_name
122: Shown to the user when they confirm the connection. Defaults to the URL's host
123: grant_types
124: Must include authorization_code. Add refresh_token to receive refresh tokens
125: response_types
126: Must be code if present
127: token_endpoint_auth_method
128: Must be none if present. Client secrets are not supported
129: Grain applies these rules to documents and their clients:
130: The URL must use https and serve the document directly, with no redirects, in at most 5 KB.
131: Grain caches the document for the max-age in its Cache-Control header, between 5 minutes and 24 hours, and revalidates it with its ETag.
132: PKCE is required, so send code_challenge in Step 2 and code_verifier when generating the token.
133: http redirect URIs are only allowed on localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1], where any port matches.
134: The workspace scope is only available to clients verified by Grain.
135: Refresh Token
136: After the access_token has expired, you may generate a new one.
137: See OAuth2 Refresh Token

16: Claude Paid Users
17: Grain MCP supports easy setup as a native Claude Integration.
18: Step 1: Integration Setup
19: Navigate to Settings → Integrations (Pro/Max Users) → Organization Settings (Team/Enterprise Users)
20: Click "+ Add Integration"
21: Enter details and click the "Add" button:
22: Integration Name: Grain
23: Integration URL: https://api.grain.com/_/mcp
24: Step 2: Connection / Authentication
25: From Settings → Integrations:
26: Look for "Grain" in the list of integrations and click "Connect"

28: Step 3: Testing MCP Tools
29: From a New Claude chat:
30: Click "Search and Tools" and confirm you can see "Grain" in the list
31: Click "Grain" to confirm the MCP tools are active, toggle tools on/off as desired
32: Test Connection by typing "Tell me about my most recent Grain meeting" or any other test prompt and Submit the chat
33: If everything is set up properly, you'll see Claude make requests to the available Grain tools that are needed to fulfill the data needs of the Chat request. For best results, turn off non-Grain tools that may distract or confuse the LLM or cite the name and filters of the Grain tool you want it to use from the Available MCP Tools section.
34: Claude Free Users & Other Clients (Developers Only)
35: 🚧
36: Please note that mcp-remote is soon to be deprecated in favor of native client integrations and as such is not an officially supported method of connection by the official Grain MCP Server. Please plan your use of this connection method accordingly.

40: Prerequisites:
41: Node.js installed (nodejs.org)

44: Open terminal/command prompt and run:
45: Copy
46: node --version

49: Edit Config File

56: "grain": {
57: "command": "npx",
58: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://api.grain.com/_/mcp"]
59: }
60: }
61: }

65: Enable Tools

67: Verify all tools are enabled
68: Allow tools when prompted in conversations
69: Test Connection:
70: Copy
71: List my recent Grain meetings
72: Personal Access Token (Developers Only)
73: Any MCP client that can send custom headers can connect with a Personal Access Token instead of OAuth.
74: This is useful for headless agents, scripts and CI, where there is no browser to complete the OAuth sign-in.
75: Generate a token from the integrations page.
76: Point your client at https://api.grain.com/_/mcp and send the token in the Authorization header:
77: Copy
78: Authorization: Bearer grain_pat_...
79: For example, with Claude Code:
80: Copy
81: claude mcp add --transport http grain https://api.grain.com/_/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer grain_pat_..."
82: The token acts as you, with the same access you have in Grain.
83: Treat it like a password, and revoke it from the integrations page if it leaks.
84: Workspace Access Tokens are not accepted by the MCP server.

evidence.observation: quote: How is API usage billed?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Billing is pay-as-you-go from a US dollar balance, and the minimum top-up is $5. Video models are priced per second of output and image models per image; DoP is the exception, priced per generation. Each model has a fixed rate for every configuration: the rate depends on settings like resolution and audio, is listed publicly, and stays the same regardless of how much you top up. An estimate endpoint returns the cost of a request before you run it. Funds expire one year after they are added to the balance. The balance can't go below zero: once it's empty, new requests wait until you add funds, or you can turn on auto top-up so production traffic never stops.

evidence.observation: quote: Q: Is it safe to use MCP servers like Grain's?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: A: MCP security relies on a trust model, and Grain's MCP server is officially supported by us and aligns with our existing security practices, follows the MCP specification exactly, and uses industry-standard OAuth authentication and HTTPS. All tool usage requires explicit user approval in Claude, and each tool request is scoped to specific data needed for that operation. While no system is 100% secure, Grain's established security practices and transparent approach to data handling make it a safer MCP implementation.

evidence.observation: quote: Q: How does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) work and what are the privacy implications?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: A: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that creates a secure bridge between Claude and external services like Grain, where your data stays in your Grain account and is only processed temporarily by Claude to answer questions. As stated by Anthropic, data accessed through MCP integrations is not used to train Claude's models.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Q: What data does Grain's MCP server have access to?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: A: Grain's MCP server only accesses data you already have permission to view in your Grain workspace, including meetings you attended, companies and contacts from those meetings, deal information (with HubSpot integration), and AI-generated notes and transcripts. It has no access to private meetings you weren't invited to or other workspaces you don't belong to. The integration uses OAuth authentication and maintains the same security boundaries as your normal Grain usage.

evidence.observation: quote: Q: How does Claude verify and approve MCP tool usage?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: A: Claude requires explicit user approval before using any Grain tool, showing you a dialog with clear descriptions of what each tool will do and offering "use once" or "use for entire session" options. Each tool requires separate approval when first used, and you maintain control over which tools Claude can access in your current session. You can revoke access by starting a new chat session, ensuring that no tools run without your explicit permission.

evidence.observation: quote: Q: Can I control what data the Grain MCP server shares with Claude?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: A: Data access is controlled through your existing Grain account permissions, and you can enable/disable specific tools in Claude's integration settings, but you cannot currently exclude specific meetings or companies from MCP access. The integration accesses all data you have permission to see in your Grain workspace and follows your existing permissions rather than providing additional filtering options. Review your Grain workspace permissions before connecting and use targeted prompts to limit the scope of data Claude requests.

Currently there's no opt-out option, but one will be available in the coming months - if you're uncomfortable with this data collection, consider waiting until then.

evidence.observation: quote: ## What is MCP?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets AI agents call external tools. An MCP server exposes a set of tools (here, Reducto's APIs) that the agent can invoke as part of its reasoning loop. You install the server once, point your client at it, and the agent figures out which tool to call and how to chain results.

Connect AI models to Otter using Model Context Protocol (MCP). Connecting Otter MCP to your AI applications enables secure, scalable access to various language model understandings to power features like smarter summaries, contextual suggestions, and automated insights for all your Otter conversations and meetings.

Learn to connect to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Perplexity, or other platforms.

What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

MCP is an open standard that allows AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT
to securely access external data sources. With Otter’s MCP Server, these AI
assistants can:

✅ Search your meeting transcripts across all time periods

✅ Analyze patterns and themes across multiple meetings

✅ Generate content using your actual meeting data

✅ Surface insights without leaving your AI workflow

🔑 Key advantage: Your meeting knowledge becomes instantly accessible to AI
assistants, eliminating manual copy-paste and context-switching.

🔒 Security: All access is OAuth-authenticated with granular permissions.
Your AI assistant can only access meetings you explicitly authorize.

Claude setup Learn how to set up Claude

Check out Otter.ai in the Claude connectors directory.

Connect Otter MCP to Claude.

  1. Go to Settings → Connectors → Browse connectors.

    Note: If your workspace admin has already added Otter.ai, it will appear as an available connector. Click Connect and proceed directly to Step 3.

  2. Go to Claude's Otter.ai page and click Connect.

  3. Sign in to your Otter account. Review the info and click Authorize access to connect with Claude.

  4. Otter MCP is connected to Claude.

Enable Otter MCP tool with chat

Click on the search and tools menu in the chat box. Toggle on Otter.

Configure your Otter MCP tool permissions

Claude will prompt for permissions when querying using Otter MCP tools.

You can manage permissions for the Otter MCP tool in the connector settings.

  1. Under the settings Connectors, click Configure next to Otter or manage through the 3-dot menu.

  2. Manage each of the tools' permissions. We recommend setting it to Always allow.

ChatGPT setup Learn how to set up ChatGPT

Connect Otter MCP to ChatGPT. Otter.ai is available in the ChatGPT App Store.

Check out Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.

  1. Sign in to the ChatGPT web version. Go to Settings.

    Note: To connect to Otter MCP, you must currently complete the connection through the web version of Otter. Connecting directly through the desktop app is not yet supported. Once the connection is established on the web, it will automatically be available in the desktop app.

  2. Go to Apps and add apps. The option may vary depending on your existing account.
  3. Go to Otter.ai in the ChatGPT App Store.
  4. Click Connect.
  5. Carefully review the information and click Connect Otter.ai.
  6. Sign in to your Otter.ai account. Carefully review the information and click Authorize access to proceed.
  7. Otter.ai is now connected to your ChatGPT account.

Enable Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT. Now that Otter is connected, you can work from the ChatGPT web browser or the desktop app.

  • Click the + (plus icon). Click ••• More and select Otter.ai.
  • Type @ and select Otter.ai.

When starting a new chat, make sure Otter.ai is showing. If you do not see otter.ai, select it again through the steps above.

Using Otter MCP tools with ChatGPT

Otter uses 3 tools in ChatGPT to query your meetings:

  • fetch
  • get user info
  • search

If prompted, accept the tool request to proceed.

You can click any source to go directly to the Otter conversation.

If you are experiencing any issues querying your Otter conversations, we recommend specifically mentioning the Otter tool you want to use in your query.

Manage Otter MCP settings for ChatGPT in Apps.

Cursor setup Learn how to set up Cursor

Connect Otter MCP to Cursor. Refer to Cursor’s documentation on connecting MCP servers for more info.

  1. Navigate to Cursor settings. Click Tools & MCP. Click Add Custom MCP.

  2. Configure the JSON file with the following. Save changes to the file.

    {
 "mcpServers": {
 "otter_meeting_mcp": {
 "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
 }
 }
}

  3. Navigate back to Tools & MCP. Click Connect.

  4. Click Open.

  5. Sign in to your Otter account. Click Authorize access.

  6. Otter MCP is connected to Cursor.

Enable Cursor

Enable Otter MCP by ensuring it's toggled ON under Cursor Tools & MCP settings and tools enabled. Cursor will automatically use available tools.

If a tool is disabled, click on the grayed-out tool to re-enable.

Perplexity Learn how to set up Perplexity

Connect Otter MCP to Perplexity using custom connectors to securely access and reference your Otter conversations, meeting notes, and AI insights directly within Perplexity.

Note: Perplexity’s UI may change over time. Refer to Perplexity’s documentation for the latest instructions on connecting a custom connector.
  1. Navigate to the Connectors settings page. The location may vary depending on whether you are using an individual or an Enterprise account.

  2. Click + Custom connector.

  3. Configure using the following settings and click Add.
    • Name: Otter.ai
    • Description: Meetings from Otter

    • MCP server URL: https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp

      Icon: The Otter icon can be downloaded here.

  4. Sign in to your Otter account and click Authorize access.

  5. Otter MCP is connected to Perplexity.

Enable Perplexity

Make sure the connector is enabled before submitting your query. You may need to grant permissions the first time you use the provided tools.

Connect Otter MCP to other AI tools You may be able to connect Otter MCP to your AI tool depending on your platform

Otter MCP can be connected to third-party AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP) using a JSON configuration file. Setup varies by platform and is managed entirely within your AI tool’s configuration. Configuration, behavior, and support depend on the specific platform you are using. Refer to your tool's documentation to connect to an MCP server.

Before you begin

  • Your AI tool must support MCP
  • You should be familiar with editing JSON configuration files
  • OAuth authentication is still required to connect

JSON Configuration file

{
 "mcpServers": {
 "otter": {
 "url": "https://mcp.otter.ai/mcp"
 }
 }
}

Complete setup in your AI tool

  1. Add a custom MCP and configure the JSON file with the above.
  2. Connect and authenticate with your Otter account.
  3. Verify the Otter MCP server appears, and tools are available.
Note: We’ll continue adding step-by-step guides for more AI tools. In the meantime, setup may vary by platform and is completed at your discretion.

# Research format and evidence rules

Contract version 1.1, 2026-11-23 (updated in Task 06 from v1.0 based on verified Task 05 pilot findings; sealed v1.0 runs retain their frozen contract snapshots).

### Changelog (v1.0 → v1.1)
- Added `vendor_approval_required` to `credential_eligibility.{testing,production}` to separate platform/vendor API-access review (e.g., Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard application) from commercial/agency `partner_approval_required`.
- Clarified edition-matching for `mcp.discovery`: a community MCP targeting a different product edition (e.g., personal web/cookie scraping vs. Enterprise REST API) must not assert `found` for the Enterprise scope without explicit edition alignment.
- Reinforced per-claim attachment: every material detail in a claim (including `purpose` and MCP tool-list observations) must be anchored inside that claim's own attached evidence array and locator line range.

## Files and migration

- `data/apps.json` is the 100-app identity roster, in assignment order. Its provenance identifies the original conversation and user turn. Original app/hint Markdown is retained verbatim, including link targets and parenthetical hints. Categories and normalized names match the audited roster.
- `legacy_candidate_doc_urls` preserves the scaffold's URL leads with their separate provenance. Neither these URLs nor assignment hints establish auth, access, API or MCP findings. Do not inherit the old OAUTH/APIKEY/GATED/MCP lists, generic descriptions, breadth placeholders or buildability labels.
- `schemas/record.json` is a Draft 2020-12 schema for one app in one immutable run. `examples/unresearched-record.json` is a format example, excluded from research and accuracy totals.
- Initialize substantive claims as `not_researched`, with null values and empty evidence. Keep prior artifacts intact as legacy material; a migration must not relabel their guesses as documentary observations. Existing scripts do not yet consume or enforce this contract.
- Paygent Connect (84) is unresolved. Preserve the original `paygent (NMI-powered)` hint. The legacy paygentglobal.com lead has no established identity match. Resolve vendor/product/edition with primary evidence before attaching that domain's facts; do not substitute a similarly named payment company. The example intentionally leaves this unresolved.

## Claim states and evidence

Each scalar claim has a stable `claim_id`, `status`, `value`, `context`, `evidence`, `supporting_claim_refs` and `rationale`. Context names the edition, API version, account type, region and environment where relevant; say which details remain unknown. IDs remain stable across revisions for the same question. Split materially different scopes into distinct method/entry claims rather than merging them.

| Status | Meaning and counting |
| --- | --- |
| `observed` | Explicitly supported by captured source content; non-null value and evidence required. This means documentary observation, not verified truth or a successful API call. |
| `inferred` | Reasoned conclusion; non-null value, evidence, rationale and supporting claim references required. Report separately from documentary observations. |
| `unknown` | Attempted investigation did not resolve the question. Null value; explain the gap. |
| `disputed` | Conflicting content has not been reconciled. Null value; at least two evidence observations and an explanation required. |
| `not_researched` | No investigation yet. Null value; never count as a finding. |
| `not_applicable` | Evidence explains why the question does not apply to the stated scope. Null value; not a negative result or a correct auth/access claim. |
| `not_found_in_checked_sources` | A bounded search found no supported result. Null value and evidence identifying checked content/search scope required. Use for MCP discovery; never translate to 'no MCP exists'. |

`coverage_status` on auth/protocol/resource collections is workflow metadata: `not_researched`, `partial`, or `checked_sources`. `checked_sources` means only the listed sources were examined, never exhaustive coverage of the vendor. Empty arrays do not prove absence. Record unresolved questions in `notes`; a researched collection can still be incomplete.

For each evidence observation record:

- The actual source URL, source kind, exact heading/anchor, page/line range, or repository path plus commit and line range in `locator`.
- A short captured observation or faithful paraphrase supporting this specific claim. A homepage URL, search-result snippet, or a whole-page citation without a locator is a lead, not substantive evidence.
- `captured_on` (ISO date), capture method, and document date/version when known. Null document metadata means unknown, not current. Capture dates must reflect actual reading, not run creation.
- SHA-256 of the captured content and a relative `snapshot_ref` where feasible. Hash normalized/extracted content only if the snapshot is exactly that content and the extraction method is recorded. If no content snapshot/hash is available, use null and a specific `hash_unavailable_reason`; do not fabricate a digest. A hash proves content identity, not correctness. Never store credentials in snapshots.

For actual operational tests, use `source_kind: execution_receipt` and `capture_method: execution_log`. These require a real local receipt/log in `snapshot_ref` and its SHA-256; `source_url` may be null for a local log. Its locator identifies the run/tool call and relevant log lines; observation states the actual result. This is the only source kind that allows a null source URL. This format permits future receipts; it implements no execution functionality and the Task 02 example has no operational findings.

Prefer vendor developer/auth/pricing/access docs and official repositories. Community repositories support their own implementation claims, not vendor endorsement. Assignment text supports identity/category/hints only. Cite approval and pricing sources for eligibility claims; an API reference alone need not establish a free credential path. If official sources conflict, preserve both observations and their time, version and scope; do not silently pick one. `conflicts` links the affected claim IDs and explains the discrepancy; `disputed` claims may also hold both observations directly.

Evidence is attached per claim. Each auth method, API protocol, resource group and MCP entry has its own claim and evidence. A shared page may be cited repeatedly with the appropriate locator. One citation must not silently support other array members or scopes. When one claim necessarily includes several details (e.g. an auth method plus documented scopes), its evidence must support every detail; otherwise split the claim or omit unestablished optional details. For review, any unsupported material detail makes that whole claim unsupported; do not inflate the denominator by splitting punctuation into claims.

## Field rules

**Identity and purpose.** `identity.id`, `app` and `category` come from the roster; resolve product identity in `identity.resolution` using a cited product/edition description. Category is assignment metadata, not a researched auth claim. `purpose` is a short, single-line, cited description. Do not put placeholder prose in an observed value.

**Auth.** `auth.items` contains a separate claim per method and scope. Preserve OAuth2, API key, Basic and tokens separately; don't choose a single winner. `context` and `details` explain API/edition/actor, OAuth grant or signing scheme; `scopes` lists only documented scopes relevant to the described use. An empty scopes list means no scopes captured, not unrestricted permissions. For CLI/local software, only assert `none` or `not_applicable` when supported for that interface; lack of a REST API does not settle CLI buildability.

**Credentials.** `credential_eligibility.testing` and `.production` each contain independent boolean claims:

- `free_access`, `trial_access`, `sandbox_access`: true means a documented credential/use path is available for this environment; false requires evidence of its absence or inapplicability. Unknown stays null.
- `paid_required`, `admin_approval_required`, `vendor_approval_required`, `partner_approval_required`, `contact_sales_required`: true means this condition is required for the stated path/scope. False needs explicit support for proceeding without it; silence is unknown. Distinguish `vendor_approval_required` (vendor/platform API-access review or application, such as Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard) from `partner_approval_required` (commercial, agency, or technology partnership program gating) and `admin_approval_required` (customer tenant/organization admin role or approval).
- `self_serve`: a documented path allows the intended developer to obtain the relevant credentials without vendor/partner intervention. A paid path may be self-serve; an existing tenant's admin can still be required. State actor/plan/prerequisites in each claim's context. Never derive this by default or from 'Sign up'.

These conditions can coexist. A free sandbox can require admin approval; production may require a paid account and partner approval. For alternative credential paths, the context of each claim must identify exactly which path it describes. Do not collapse conflicting paths to one app-wide boolean: use unknown/disputed with explanatory evidence until a scoped answer is possible. A paid product does not automatically mean API access is gated, and a free trial does not establish production access.

**API surface.** Protocols, public documentation, resource groups and breadth are independent claims. A known REST protocol must survive even when breadth and resource groups are unknown. Record each documented protocol and resource group separately with supporting sections; a source can establish 'contacts' while leaving 'billing' unresearched. `public_documentation` refers to documentation visibility for this API scope, not credential eligibility or public data access. Public documentation does not mean anonymous API access.

`breadth` is an inference supported by resource-group claim IDs: `narrow` = one focused workflow/group; `moderate` = multiple related groups; `broad` = multiple distinct business domains. Explain the classification and captured examples in context/rationale. This is qualitative scope, not a fabricated endpoint inventory or a guarantee of completeness. Leave unknown if not enough resource documentation was read. REST/GraphQL/SDK/CLI can coexist; include other interfaces when relevant to agent-callable tools.

**MCP.** `mcp.discovery` is `observed` with value `found` only when at least one supported entry matching the record's declared product edition/scope is recorded. A community MCP targeting a separate consumer/personal edition (e.g., undocumented web-cookie scraping) does not establish `found` for an Enterprise API scope unless tested and documented for that edition; preserve such community entries only with explicit edition separation or leave Enterprise MCP discovery `not_found_in_checked_sources`/`unknown`. Otherwise use the appropriate null state. Each `mcp.entries` item is its own claim with `official`/`community`, source URL, scope, and repository/server URL where established (null otherwise). A server URL may be a hosted endpoint, while a local stdio server may have only a repository URL. No guessed URL. Vendor endorsement must be supported to call it official. Entries for outgoing MCP clients do not establish an app's callable server; record tool direction/scope. `operational_check` remains `not_researched` unless actual execution logs support the result. Docs, a server listing, or a GitHub README cannot establish successful connection, tool calls, or production readiness. This task runs no operational checks.

**Buildability.** This is an explicit inference for a stated agent workflow: `build_now`, `conditional`, `outreach_required` or `not_buildable_for_stated_scope`. Cite supported identity/auth/access/API/MCP or CLI claims through `supporting_claim_refs`, include relevant source evidence, explain the conclusion, list blockers and next steps. A public API can still require outreach; no MCP alone is not a blocker to building an API wrapper. Unknown identity/access/API details can leave buildability unknown. `build_now` is feasibility from evidence, not an implemented or tested integration. Blocker statements also require support; do not label an app unbuildable because a fetch failed.

## Fetch telemetry is separate

`fetches` records URL, attempt date, status, HTTP status, resolved URL, error and optional content digest. It never supplies claim truth. DNS/HTTP errors, login walls, robots blocks and timeouts do not establish no API, paid access, partner gating or nonexistent MCP. A 200 response does not establish a cited claim. Fetch outcomes can prompt follow-up but cannot promote research states automatically.

## Review, runs and accuracy

1. Every saved run gets a unique `run_id`, creation date and producer identity/type. Persist the run input roster hash, schema/rules versions, tool/model versions and configuration alongside that run in a run manifest. Never reuse a run ID or overwrite original records, evidence snapshots, logs or adjudications. The example's run ID is illustrative only.
2. Corrections create a new run with `parent_run_id` and `correction_refs` naming original run/claim IDs plus reasons. Keep the original value/evidence unchanged in the parent; revised claims reuse the same question ID where scope is unchanged. Record added/removed/split claims explicitly in the correction log. New evidence does not retroactively become first-pass evidence.
3. `review` is pending until actual claim adjudications exist. Completed means the listed adjudications are completed, not that every field/app was reviewed. Capture reviewer ID, `ai` or `human`, date, original run ID, each claim ID, judgment, rationale and review evidence. A tool/browser action or another AI is still AI review; only an actual identified person can sign human review. Producer and reviewer identities must be distinct for independent review; disclose shared model/context. Do not copy pending entries over completed reviews.

   An `unresolved` judgment may have an empty evidence array when no source content could be captured. Its required reason must name the actual fetch attempt (for example `fetches[0]` and its date/URL) or an existing failure-log path and describe why adjudication could not finish. Runtime review must resolve that reference. Do not fabricate a source observation for a DNS/access failure. `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported` and `not_applicable` judgments still require captured evidence; a failure-only review cannot establish any of them. A completed review containing unresolved judgments does not mean those claims have been verified and contributes no accuracy denominator for those judgments.
4. Before full-run verification, freeze a sampling manifest: manifest ID/path, target run, roster SHA-256, selection date, method/algorithm/version, seed, selected IDs, category counts, reviewer assignments and claim rubric. Use a deterministic seeded selection of two apps per category (20 total), without replacement; report all ten categories including Support and Helpdesk. Preserve pilot/targeted reviews separately from this sample. A seed alone does not reproduce an unspecified algorithm. Do not select actual sample IDs in Task 02.
5. Freeze the claim inventory and scoring rubric before review. Unit = each non-null `observed` or `inferred` claim object, identified by `(run_id, app_id, claim_id)`. Count auth methods, protocols, groups and MCP entries separately; nested operational checks are separate claims only if asserted. Score a compound claim correct only if all material details hold for its scope. Report documentary and inference results separately. Category/roster metadata, example fixtures, collection metadata, null states and bare URLs are not scored findings.
6. Each adjudication is `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported`, `unresolved`, or `not_applicable`. Unsupported is a failure to substantiate, not proof of factual falsity. Let C/I/U be completed correct/incorrect/unsupported judgments for asserted claims. Evidence-backed accuracy = C / (C + I + U); print those counts, with unresolved/pending/excluded totals alongside. If the denominator is zero, accuracy is null ('unmeasured'), not 0% or 100%. Exclude null-state claims and not-applicable judgments from this accuracy denominator; report any invalid applicability claims as audit issues. Do not drop incorrect or unsupported results after correction.
7. Report review coverage = completed C/I/U judgments / eligible asserted claims in the frozen sample, with unresolved and pending counts. Separately report research coverage across all 100: counts of observed, inferred and each null state for the six required research areas (purpose, auth, credentials, API, MCP, buildability), plus identity resolution. A collection is not covered just because it exists; distinguish partial protocol knowledge from missing breadth. Report area completion criteria and every denominator. Unknowns do not count as correct findings. No one overall 'accuracy' number should conceal missing research or missing review.
8. First-pass and corrected scores refer to immutable runs, the same sample and the frozen claim questions. Link changed/removed/split/new questions; publish paired results on comparable questions and the changed inventory separately. Do not claim improvement by deleting hard claims, changing denominators or relabeling a failure unknown. A corrected/previously reviewed sample is not an unbiased held-out estimate; disclose reuse. Report no accuracy or improvement until actual adjudication exists. Prepare a human checklist if no person has reviewed yet; do not claim human checks were performed.

## Publication contract (later tasks only)

A hosting config, Site registration, expected URL, local Git directory or ZIP is not proof of publication. Save a repository creation/write receipt, actual repository URL, commit SHA, source/README existence and readback evidence. Save the deployment ID/status, actual live URL, deployed commit or artifact SHA-256, date, and an independent fetch/browser result demonstrating the page is accessible to the intended reviewer. Record real errors/blockers when unsuccessful. No publication is attempted in Task 02.

## Validation and Task 03 handoff

No dependencies were installed. From the workspace root, the available PowerShell validates the example:

```powershell
Test-Json -Path examples/unresearched-record.json -SchemaFile schemas/record.json
$roster = Get-Content -Raw data/apps.json | ConvertFrom-Json
if ($roster.apps.Count -ne 100) { throw 'Expected 100 apps' }
if (($roster.apps.id -join ',') -ne ((1..100) -join ',')) { throw 'IDs/order changed' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category).Count -ne 10) { throw 'Expected 10 categories' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category | Where-Object Count -ne 10).Count) { throw 'Expected 10 apps per category' }
```

If `jsonschema` is already installed in another environment, this optional check verifies both the schema and example (do not install it for this task):

```console
python -c "import json,jsonschema; s=json.load(open('schemas/record.json')); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator.check_schema(s); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(s, format_checker=jsonschema.FormatChecker()).validate(json.load(open('examples/unresearched-record.json'))); print('valid')"
```

Schema validation enforces required fields, value types, explicit states, local evidence minimums for assertions, reference presence for inferences, and pending/completed review shape. It cannot establish source truth, identity, evidence relevance, all reference integrity, actual human activity, or immutable run history. Validators may treat `format` as annotation: Task 03 must explicitly validate URLs/date values.

Runtime/reviewer checks to implement in Task 03 (not implemented here):

- Match IDs/names/categories to the roster; unresolved identity blocks promotion of product-specific claims.
- Ensure unique claim IDs (including nested checks), resolve all support/conflict/adjudication/correction references, reject self/circular support, and ensure buildability/breadth dependencies are supported and scoped consistently. Referenced IDs are claim IDs within this app/run unless explicitly paired with an original run ID.
- Require each asserted method/group/server and every material detail to be supported by its own evidence; inspect the actual cited content. Do not accept assignment hints or legacy leads as product evidence. `breadth` must use `inferred` and reference resource claims; `not_found_in_checked_sources` is restricted to MCP discovery.
- Require no asserted items under `not_researched` collection status; track partial knowledge and source scope. MCP `found` needs at least one supported entry and source-backed origin; operational success needs execution receipts. No nonempty MCP entries under an unknown/negative discovery state.
- Verify valid dates/URLs, content hashes/snapshot paths, document versions, primary/community attribution and conflicts. Keep fetch failures separate and ensure captures correspond to real reads.
- Enforce append-only runs/reviews and snapshot storage, parent/correction linkage, review identity/type, sample reproducibility/category coverage, frozen claim denominators and metric arithmetic. Retain unsupported results.
- Require publication receipts/readback before reporting repo/live-page success.

Coordinator acceptance should cover: honest unknown example passes; multi-auth and REST-only partial knowledge pass; evidence-free observed auth/purpose and unsupported inferred buildability fail; malformed dates/refs are flagged by runtime if the validator does not reject them; completed review with no reviewer/judgments fails. Passing a schema is not evidence that Task 03 or the assignment research is complete.

roster.purpose: Assignment identity inputs and source leads only; no researched app findings.

provenance.method: Original user assignment read via read_thread; hints preserved verbatim as Markdown; normalized app names, IDs, categories and order checked against research_agent.py RAW. No websites fetched.
provenance.legacy_warning: Candidate URLs are unverified source leads, not original assignment hints or evidence. Legacy auth/access/API/MCP/buildability guesses are excluded.

apps.identity_note: Original hint is paygent (NMI-powered). No evidence links this product to paygentglobal.com. Do not endorse that domain, substitute another Paygent product, or attach its docs until primary evidence resolves the identity.
